subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 20, consideration of the motion of Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have now had some days in which the public has been able to take stock of the budget presented by the Minister of Finance on Tuesday night and it seems to me there has been a singular unanimity with
23, 1956
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell regard to it. The unanimity was perhaps best expressed by a sports broadcaster, I believe, who said on the air last evening that in the budget the score was 0-0. I hope, Mr. Speaker, it will be realized that this fact makes my task difficult. It is difficult to make a dent in a rubber ball and it is difficult to make bricks without straw; but I must simply do my best.
It is, of course, obvious to everyone, and indeed I am not sure it has not already been said, that this is not a budget at all but a prologue to a budget. This is merely holding the line. Of course next year we will hear the story. We are all familiar with the saying of the great French king who said, "L'Etat, c'est moi." However, I doubt if he ever carried it quite so far as this government carries it. It seems to me that what is happening now makes it clear that in the minds of the government they believe that their remaining in office is a matter of supreme importance, not only to themselves but apparently somehow or other they have made themselves believe that it is important to Canada as well. I do not know how they do that.
In effect what they do is to come to the taxpayers and say, "We are in a very comfortable position, thank you; we have $26 billion gross national product and that leaves us in a good position because it means that taxes have rolled in abundantly, beyond what we could have asked or thought; so we are able to tell you the taxpayers, that there is no need to increase your taxes; however, on the other hand you realize that to lower your taxes now would be quite childish foolishness; what is the use of our lowering them now, the time to lower them is next year."
Admittedly the minister cannot say that and I have to say it for him. There are a lot of people saying it for him and I would like to associate myself with them. He is in a difficult position. I suppose if he had had his own way he would not have made a speech at all, he would have just made a little announcement as to one or two changes. However, you cannot do that very well. After all, the minister has to have his flower in his buttonhole, he has to make an entry into the house, he has to be received, he has to be photographed; that is all part of the performance, that is all part of public relations and nobody should complain.
What did we have? We had some amiable generalities about the economic position. I think the minister was a little cramped by the fact that the Gordon commission has been asked to become the brains of the government and therefore he had to be a little cautious about what he said. Then we

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell had an apologia for the arrangement with the provinces, but I am not going to go into that. I am only going to quote the homely words of the premier of Ontario which seemed to me to be an apt commentary on all the philosophical hair-splitting that we had from the minister the other day. I liked what the premier of Ontario said, that the government had just rolled over in bed and given us what we were entitled to. That seemed to me to put it most tellingly. Perhaps if the minister had thought of those words he would have used them himself.
I just want to make one other comment on dominion-provincial relations. It is of course quite clear that we are still in the realm of doles, that we have not yet grappled with the problem which is not to make grants to the provinces but to set up the provinces on their own feet and give them a chance to be self-sustaining. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) shakes his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was just hoping my hon. friend would go on and explain how that could be done.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall have a word or two to say about that. It could only be done if there were an entirely new approach to the whole thing. I agree that there has to be something done that has never been attempted in the philosophy of this government, particularly vis-a-vis the maritimes. I agree with the minister on that, and I shall say more later. I shall say no more about dominion-provincial relations. I just repeat that unfortunately we are left in the position where we can conclude that the government had concentrated on their own affairs and not on those of the community, particularly those elements in the community which, as I shall point out, are in distress.
I should think that private members on the government side, who came down here, I am sure, with the idea that they were serving the public, must be taken aback by that. On the other hand, of course, they no doubt are getting the one-party mind. They are reminded they have been here 20 years. It is wonderful how often we have to go back to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but then he says so many interesting things. It is rumoured that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has told them that if they are good boys there is no reason why they should not be down here for 50 years.
We must be fair. We must admit that the government has not always been as inefficient as it has been in the last couple of months. We have to admit that they do show a certain efficiency in approaching the election issue. So the people of Canada must wait, and then a new light will appear, probably from the


Minister of National Health and Welfare, and they will be offered new inducements paid for with their own money.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You seem to be worried about the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have known the Minister of National Health and Welfare a long time and I have watched with great interest his progress in different ways, and I am sure he will not mind my commenting on it. These electoral inducements are interesting, and I hope both the electors and the press will pay great attention to them. We discovered a year ago, what perhaps we were in danger of forgetting, how powerful the press can be. And I hope they will show themselves powerful again.
As I listened to the minister and his explanation of the income for this year and next year, I was reminded of a remark that I think his predecessor made once, to the effect that government receipts and disbursements were flexible things and that it mattered a good deal whether a payment or a disbursement was made just before or after the end of the fiscal year. I wondered whether perhaps the minister had that in mind and whether in his innocent way, because after all he is innocent, he might have done something in the way of accelerating or delaying payments. I wonder if the minister thought of that. I wonder if perhaps he made this empty budget still a little more empty in order that there might be a larger and more fertilizing flood to be let loose next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perish the thought.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At any rate this is an empty budget. Somebody has called it a Mother Hubbard budget, and certainly I think the cupboard is bare enough as far as the taxpayers are concerned this year. But that is because the government must have glittering prizes next year. Health is often mentioned as the ace of trumps for next summer. But there are reassuring signs of criticism in the press, signs that these slick tactics are not wholly approved.
I think I would have taken all of this more or less in good part, and I would not have felt indignant about it, as I do feel, if in fact throughout Canada we had no elements among the taxpayers who were suffering, but I believe we have and I believe there has been a notable failure on the part of this government to attempt to deal with what I would call the soft spots.
Although they have a roaring boom in the United States they are trying to deal with the soft spots, but I want to put a word in here as earnestly as I can for the hundreds of thousands in Canada who are not getting

a fair share. There is not a word of cheer for them in the budget, not even a recognition of their problem. They are the forgotten men and women. What about the unemployed? What about the maritimes? What about the textile workers? What about the rapid buying up of Canadian companies which is causing serious alarm in many circles? These problems are not dealt with. They are not even recognized. Why the neglect? Well, it might be answered that the Gordon commission is going to settle everything, but after all, all that the Gordon commission can do is make a report. In all likelihood, what it will do is to touch off more political discussion, and to say that those who need adjustments are going to wait for months and months while that is done is to talk political nonsense.
No doubt the report of the commission will be made before the election. No doubt it will be regarded as another trump card, but that is not to say that the things which should be done are going to be done in a hurry. At the present time the commission is head over heels in work. It has received, of course, scores and scores of briefs and it is now employing probably scores of economists who are working for it and producing further material.
The budget was not an interesting budget but there were one or two interesting things in it. I want to mention one in particular. One thing I liked very much was that the minister went out of his way to make flattering remarks about certain of his colleagues and really tried to create the impression that the cabinet is now a band of brothers. One does not know whether that is true. Rumours do get about, but at any rate I should like to draw attention to the fact that the minister rather went out his way, I thought, to refer to some of his fellow members of the cabinet. I did not know whether he was preaching for a call. I did observe that those who were referred to were, if I may venture to say so, not very likely contestants at the next party convention. At any rate, I do not want to impute any motives to the minister and I will simply read the references and let them speak for themselves.
The first one was with regard to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). As I said a few minutes ago, how we do come back to the Minister of Trade and Commerce! I hope he does not mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am neutral in this debate. Why pick on me?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know the minister does not approve of many debates and maybe he does not approve of this one, but I know he will forgive me for any references I may
23,	1956	2543
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell make to him. It is only because one meets him going and coming and one gets very familiar with him. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), in referring to his own optimistic predictions of a year ago, said, as found at page 2325 of Hansard of March 20:
As a matter of fact, at a later time during the year, someone wrote that he could only conclude that some of the optimism of the Minister of Trade and Commerce had rubbed off on the new Minister of Finance. I would like to say that I would be happy if other qualities of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were also to rub off on me.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which ones?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is a pleasant compliment but it also imposes a heavy responsibility on the minister if he is going to become a model to all the younger men in the cabinet. Of course it made me think, what would the cabinet be like if it were full of C. D. Howes? That is a very interesting question to me. I remember somebody saying years ago, would it not be a wonderful thing if you could have the 265 ablest men in Canada all elected to the House of Commons. Some other man, shrewder and wiser, said that it would make government absolutely impossible because each one would want to be the leader. As I say, what kind of a cabinet it would be I do not pretend to guess. I would be inclined to say, what price democracy if you had a cabinet full of masterful people like the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), but that is as it may be.
Now then, next we have a reference to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). The Minister of Finance says, "May I express my appreciation to the Minister of National Revenue and his staff for collecting such a tremendous sum of money." The minister does, indeed, collect a tremendous sum of money, but of course he does this as the agent of the Minister of Finance. I repeat what I said the other evening that the minister who 18 months ago expressed awe at the power he had has quickly got used to it. It gets them all, this spending habit.
Now, the Minister of Finance went on to speak about the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). We were told the Prime Minister has lived with the problems of dominion-provincial relations for some 18 years, ever since he became counsel for the Rowell-Sirois commission. I have no doubt the Prime Minister was a very able counsel to the Rowell-Sirois commission, but I am quite confident that the Prime Minister had many other things on his mind, if not then certainly since that time. It seems to me a rather pleasant exaggeration to say that he has lived with these problems, because after all he was at

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell one time minister of justice and at another time secretary of state for external affairs. Then, we have the reference to the Minister of Justice. As to that, I would say that since he left Manitoba I think we have come to regard him as one of the great centralizers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I hope I may be forgiven, but this handing out of bouquets turns my mind back two or three years ago to a very interesting incident in this house when, for some reason that I have never found quite clear to my mind, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) launched out in praise of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and himself. He enunciated a theory which may be interesting even now, because after all the reference to the Prime Minister made then may still be very much in point. I think if we look back to what has happened during this session we may hope very much that it is in point. The Minister of Agriculture said this as far back as 1951, as reported at page 2046 of Hansard for April 16, 1951:
As long as the three of us-
That is the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister.
-remain where we are I think it will be fairly generally agreed across the country that we have an exceedingly good government.
Now, I envy the minister for being able to say that. I wish I were able to feel as pleased with myself as that. At any rate, there it is and it speaks for itself.
Then, he goes on to make what to many of us may seem an even more interesting comment. He said, "One of the reasons why we are satisfied to be where we are is because we both know we can afford to make statements, knowing that we might be incorrect, because we have a leader who does not make many mistakes." I was very interested in that because it seemed to indicate a situation where it did not matter very much what the other members of the cabinet did so long as there was a Prime Minister there who did not make many mistakes. This seemed to me to be a kind of blessed irresponsibility which I think is very comforting to the other members of the cabinet.
I come now to speak about some of the forgotten men and women. I wish to say a word about unemployment. Everyone will remember, I think it is less than two years ago, September, 1954, in fact, when the Prime Minister launched out and made a statement which sounded like a kind of clarion call. He said, "We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize

the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent-"

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He goes on to say, "I cannot give details but I am convinced that if my colleagues and I cannot organize economic controls in such a way that there will not be any long periods of loss of work for those who want to work, then throw us out and put in our place people who can do better." That was the Prime Minister's statement. As I say, it was a kind of clarion call but the voice of the trumpet was not so clear when the Prime Minister got back to the House of Commons. In January, he was not quite taking the same line. In January, 1955, he said this, and this seems to me like rather the feeble voice of the flute as compared with the trumpet. "There is some unemployment in Canada. There has been some unemployment in Canada every year. That situation has eased as the season advanced and there is reason to expect that it will do so again." Now, that seems to me a very disappointing outcome.
I shall quote a few figures to show what the situation is this year. It is bad enough, but not as bad as a year ago. The figures this year are, however, in all conscience, bad enough. In February, 1956, unplaced applicants were 515,000, almost 100,000 less than 1955 but 113,000 more than in 1953. Those without jobs and seeking work numbered 308,000, almost 70,000 less than a year ago but approximately the same as 1954. No one could be happy with those figures, but what is being done about it? Here are the words of the Minister of Labour: "I hope and believe we are learning many things which will be useful to us in the future."
It is interesting to note that in the United States they do not act in this negative manner. They really try to do something. They have soft spots there. They use various means to deal with chronic unemployment. Incidentally, they have been trying to help small businesses, too, which has an impact on unemployment. They have an organization that does that which has made 1,645 loans in the last period with an expenditure of $83 million. Now, that is the attitude which they have and so far as we are concerned it seems to me we must call the government back to duty. We must remind them that these are fellow citizens who are entitled to be considered, and that it does not help them very much to be told that we expect this year a G.N.P. of $28 billion. They are not interested in billions, millions, thousands or even hundreds. What they are interested in is being able to earn their day to day living as self-respecting men and women.

I wish now to say a word about the maritimes and I wish to stress that as strongly as I can. I feel very deeply about it. Here again we need an entirely new approach. It is not surprising that people from the maritimes say that when they come up to a meeting in central Canada they feel like poor relations. They feel they are not wanted. One of them said he felt almost as though he got a slap in the face. Here again, so far as I can see, there is no intention of grappling with the problem seriously. All that is being done is that the maritimes are being given a subsidy to put them off, to keep them quiet. This has been the case, notwithstanding the years of huge expenditures. If ever there was a time when industries could have been set up in the maritimes it was within the last few years. What we want is a new look, not palliatives and not one commission after another, each doing a little tinkering and recommending concessions in railway rates or other concessions. We want a new approach.
After all, confederation was a great act of faith and imagination but it did not, in itself, assure an adequate and effective economic background for the federal system. It was clear from the outset that the maritimes were taking far more risk than the rest of us. They were jeopardizing their north and south trade to a far greater extent than the rest of Canada was. Happily, in the early years, there was prosperity, which helped confederation on its way. Britain was booming; the United States was undergoing great railway expansion and there was for a few years satisfactory prosperity. The people of the maritimes look back on that now as a kind of golden age that they can hardly remember, and especially when times are prosperous in central Canada and the rest of Canada. They feel, and let no one be surprised, that they have not had a fair deal.
I have known this, of course, but it has been rubbed into me; it has been impressed on me far more than ever before by things which have been used in this House of Commons recently. The member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) said a thing a few weeks ago which startled me. He said, as reported at page 378 of Hansard'.
For more than 80 years confederation has hung like a killing blight over the economy of the maritimes.
A killing blight, Mr. Speaker.
Now, he might soften that remark a little; he might lessen the 80 years a little because the first few years were prosperous, but when a serious man who has served his country both in peace and war can use language of
23, 1956	2545
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell that kind, then I say it is time for the rest of us to have a new look.
I shall now give a few figures as to the economic position, but before I do that I want to remind the house that not so long ago, I think it was the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) who said that men had gone from the maritimes to New Zealand looking for work. That is a thing which every hon. member should regard as a personal responsibility of his own to prevent.
Let me give a few figures as to the economic comparison. In the three maritime provinces in 1946 the income per member of the labour force was $307, or 15 per cent below the national average. By 1949 the difference was $573, or 23-1 per cent. By 1953, it was $770, or 22-7 per cent. If we took this percentage at so much per head the disparity would be greater than that.
Let me give one or two figures as at the present moment. If we take unplaced applicants as the percentage of labour supply in February, 1956, we find that the percentage for the whole of Canada is 11-7. For the three maritime provinces it is 17-5 per cent, and for the four Atlantic provinces it is 19 per cent. The figure for persons without jobs and seeking work as a percentage of labour supply for the whole of Canada is 7 per cent; for the three maritime provinces it is 11-1 per cent; and for the four Atlantic provinces it is 10-8 per cent. These are figures, Mr. Speaker, which should strike every one of us and which should be intolerable for us to hear. We should never rest until we have remedied the condition.
There was an excellent debate in this house the other night, and I should like to paraphrase one or two of the things that were said because, happily, during the debate views were expressed on all sides of the house. Maritime members on all sides of the house stood up and expressed themselves. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Mac-Eachen) had something like this to say. He said that he believed we were really following a great historical tradition when we talk about policies which may serve to build up areas of Canada which up to the present time have not participated in our prosperity in the manner that we all desire. Later on, the hon. member said-and I commend this especially to members of the government:
It is through acceleration, with present government services directed with greater intensity to what might be called special areas that much can be done.
How true that is, and how absent we find any suggestion of intensity. That is what we need. As I say, we need a new look.

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
I am happy to say that the premier of Ontario has expressed himself in no uncertain way in this matter. It is a question for this house, and I hope the debate will continue as a top priority problem, and that hon. members on all sides will express themselves. That will be the only way to cure the lethargy, to inspire the indifference, and to show the government the way to action.
The minister asks me for a way to do it. I have no detailed plan of how to do it but what I am saying is this. The first prerequisite as to how to do it is to believe it is necessary that it should be done, and I am quite satisfied there is no such belief in the government at the present time.
Now, let me give a word from Mr. Frost. I am quoting from the Globe and Mail of March 10, and this is a Canadian Press report:
Mr. Frost was particularly concerned about the future of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
I was glad to read that. I am afraid that sometimes in Ontario we do not appear as interested as we should be; therefore, I was glad to read this from Mr. Frost. I continue:
For these two provinces Mr. Frost had earlier urged an annual federal subsidy of $10 million each.
This amount, really very little by comparison with what the federal government takes out of the provinces, spells the difference between prosperity and depression for these maritime provinces.
It will not be too long before the federal government regrets the action it took today.
Added to this comment is a further one from Premier Frost which represents an overall expression of the premier's position with regard to the federal government's proposal:
They were wrong in 1945; they were wrong in 1952, and they are wrong today.
Not only the premier of Ontario, but another provincial premier has expressed his alarm at the way the shoulder of the federal government is turned to the maritime provinces. There was a Canadian Press dispatch of March 13, but I have not it here. It was a statement by the premier of Saskatchewan also agreeing that the maritimes should be more fairly dealt with.
In his report to congress of last November the president, among other things, said that much had been done to improve and stimulate the United States economy. He referred to the curtailing of government activities that could be handled as well or better by private enterprise. He is following the advice that Churchill gave not so long ago in telling the govern-to "get out of the way". In that connection, I want to say a word about Trans-Canada Air Lines. I want to do this because it is clear that there is a widespread feeling across Canada, as shown by the press, that this

monopoly should come to an end. It really has become a case of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) v. Canada. I wish to put in several quotes from the press across the country. We have heard a great deal from our government about preserving private enterprise and competition, but let us look at their actions. Here is what the Winnipeg Free Press has to say:
It is high time that the government's policy on transcontinental air service was changed so that Canadians from coast to coast may enjoy the benefits which would accrue from T.C.A. having a little competition.
Arthur Blakely, writing in the Montreal Gazette, said:
It is quite clear that trade minister C. D. Howe who maintains a fatherly interest in all crown corporations will fight tooth and nail for the preservation of the monopoly. He would, if that were possible, be even less enthusiastic about any proposal to sell T.C.A. on the open market for a price however reasonable.
Not all of Mr. Howe's cabinet colleagues, it is reported, are as disturbed at the thought of breaking the monopoly. But unless parliament forces a showdown no such development is likely to take place while he remains in the cabinet.
A similar view is expressed by the Vancouver Province:
In theory it is that all transcontinental flying shall be reserved for Trans-Canada Air Lines but in practice it is that T.C.A.'s monopoly shall cover all east-west flying whether it is a through transcontinental run or not.
As we have argued before in these columns the theoretical policy may be defensible but the practice is not.
Its result was to prevent Canadian Pacific Airlines from supplying a freight service which T.C.A. did not then offer. Its result now is to deprive a number of cities of a low-cost short haul passenger service which T.C.A. does not now offer.
In theory the policy is protective, in practice it is restrictive.
And, finally, a quotation from the Ottawa Citizen:
There was good reason lor the T.C.A. monopoly when it was granted 18 years ago . . .
But in the intervening years T.C.A. has grown and prospered to the point where it is now scarcely able to handle the demand. Air traffic will most certainly continue to increase in the years to come and in the citizens' view it is time another carrier helped with the load.
It is interesting to note that the Minister of Finance was quoted the other day as saying in Brantford that "in a free enterprise economy it is not the function of the government to interfere actively with the natural direction of economic development."
I wish to say a word about commonwealth trade. On various occasions this party has tried to bring this to the attention of the house. We have made motions which have always been turned down. We have tried our best to keep this before the government but without much success. One would think

that now, with the hundreds of millions of deficit, with the $840 million deficit on current account which we had with the United States last year, the desire to explore every avenue of trade would be strong in the government; and yet, in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) on this point, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to our amazement, said that the Department of Trade and Commerce was doing nothing about it. Can anyone tell why? We certainly need external markets. Is there some fatal lethargy?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think that is quite
fair. The question did not ask what we were doing about trade but what we were doing about the adverse trade balance with the United States.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will accept the minister's correction, but what we are talking about is certainly concerned with trade and I want to be fair. Is it because we do not want to play ball with the other members of the commonwealth? Surely they could do more business with us and surely it should be explored in every possible way. There has never been a satisfactory answer. We are just left to suppose that everything that can be done is being done by an allwise government, but it is not as simple as that.
Not long ago we moved a resolution to the effect that this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of inviting the nations of the commonwealth to a conference to be held in the immediate future for the purpose of working out arrangements to preserve and enlarge those traditional markets on which jobs and opportunities for Canadians very largely depend. In that connection I would like to quote from that well-known authority, Dr. W. A. Mackintosh of Queen's University, who, when writing of the United States performance under GATT in the Foreign Affairs Quarterly of last October, said:
There are signs that we are entering a period when other countries may press American representatives to produce evidence that the United States is able to make a dependable agreement. To say this is not to discount the ingenious and sincere efforts which have been made by President Eisenhower to further the aim of larger and more competitive trade in the western world. But Congress rules. In future, however, if agreements are to be subject to the heavy discount of escape clauses and modifying legislation a much greater consideration may be required.
Dr. Mackintosh also points out that the most moderate restriction of trade in the United States, having regard to the enormous size of their business, may be of decisive importance in Canada in respect of Canadian exports. When he said that, he was speaking
23. 1956
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell of cereals; but it applies right across the board as well. We know perfectly well that the United States has not fully grown up in respect of its economic responsibility, at any rate not in tariff matters. We know they will put up tariffs as soon as anyone at home is being hit. I remind you of what I said a moment ago concerning Dr. Mackintosh's query about a "dependable agreement." We also have to remind ourselves that, the United States not being under a responsible form of government, their executive cannot deal firmly and decisively and cannot make agreements which they are perfectly sure of being able to carry through.
There is another problem I wish to raise and that is a problem which is coming more and more to our minds particularly by reason of recent United States legislation. I refer to the invasion of United States shareholders. Indeed, there is now a new phrase, "Dollar colonialism", which has crept into the language. We welcome United States capital to Canada, of course, but it must be brought here on some fair basis. Recent events have caused great heart searching. United States investment in Canadian companies has grown very rapidly. It is pointed up by recent action in five of the states where they have sought to exclude a Canadian company, although happily in one state the governor has vetoed it.
This matter has been of serious concern to the business world in Canada and we get no lead from the government. What it really means is that Canadian investors are being frozen out in respect of United States companies. One-third of the investment in Canadian manufacturing is in companies controlled outside of Canada, United States companies. Some of them are wholly owned, there are subsidiaries in many cases, and the Canadian investor has no chance to invest. The number of companies controlled has grown from 1,985 at the end of the war to 3,235 in 1953. And do not let us imagine that these are small companies. Most of them are large and some of them are huge. A good many of our commodities are now controlled by the United States. A partial list includes iron ore, nickel, aluminum, oil, copper and asbestos, all of which are under effective United States control.
Is there any disadvantage to this? Yes, there is a very great disadvantage and it grows and grows and can become very acute if anything less than a roaring boom is occurring in the United States, because, as I said, they take immediate steps to protect their own people if there is any trouble at

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell home. A witness appearing before the royal commission on patents said:
Canadian Industries Limited was not permitted by its U.S. and U.K. parents to export from Canada. Similarly Canadian radio manufactures, titanium processors, optical goods manufacturers, and many, many others, have been compelled in this way to refrain from assisting in the development of Canadian export trade.
That could toe expanded, but I shall not take up more time of the house in doing that. Why have we heard nothing of this? Why is it not stressed? Of course the Americans are within their rights in coming in and buying, but they are sensible people and there is no reason why that situation cannot be discussed with them. We could argue for good customer relations. After all, if Canadian purchasers came to know the situation they could easily lay off buying from these companies; nor is there any reason why there should not be fair regulation. Dr. Mackintosh, speaking of this, says:
Recently there have been some murmurs of complaint that certain areas of Canadian industry and finance are powerfully affected by United States subsidiaries in which there is no Canadian share in management . . . and no full reporting on the results of the Canadian sector of the enterprise.
Now I come to our old friend, the question of extravagance and waste. I remember several years ago, when our budget was about $2,400 million, the then Minister of Finance said to us that we could not expect to have the budget reduced as long as we wanted to have the services we were then getting. That was certainly a conservative statement. We must remember that was before the days of huge defence expenditures. Of course today we are having services we never dreamed of before. The Department of National Health and Welfare notably will not forget anything, because a vote is a vote. Incidentally, the independent health organizations, I think, find it hard, or believe it is hard, to get assistance from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). He prefers to dole out the money himself and I suppose his argument would toe, "Well, they are not looking for votes and I am, therefore it is so much better to have this go out with he slogan: This comes to you from the Minister of National Health and Welfare."
As I said the other evening, we have a pamphlet on baby talk and there is also one on jealousy. Then I am interested in noting that the minister is interested in the stage because there is a pamphlet, issued in connection with the stage, which so far as I can make out is produced by his department. Then when we come to the Department of Fisheries we find that they issue a pamphlet


on "ways to cook fish." Then there is one with the mysterious title "Oceans of Goodness". At any rate "oceans" fits in with the Department of Fisheries and I suppose it is all right.
But the Canadian taxpayer pays for all this. We can see that the Minister of Finance has given up. I said the other evening, and I shall not repeat, that he came to us recommended as a great, strong, rugged, unyielding, tough and unpleasant fellow who was going to crack down on all departments. But that has not happened and it will not happen. There is only one way that there will ever be any economy and that is for the minister to make up his mind as to how much a department should have and then tell them that that is all they are going to get and let them spend it as they see fit. I believe he would then see amazing instances of economy. As it is, the minister is beaten before he begins. Members of the department come all keyed up ready to prove that they need what they want to get. I suggest again to the minister that the present system is futile, that he could work miracles if he said to the department, "There is your allotment, if you want some special project you can make any economies yourself and get it." I believe that that could be done.
Of course the suspicion enters my mind that our ministers of finance themselves are not really crusaders for economy. I have never been able to believe that. After all, the expenditure of money makes them popular with a good many people, and large expenditures of billions help to increase the gross national product and help to create for the moment a buoyant situation. They help to add to the minister's taxes, and there you are. The merry-go-round goes on and on; some people think it can go on forever, but I am not one of those. I again put it to the minister with the greatest confidence that the only solution which will bring about economy is the one I have suggested.
I should like to give special mention again to the Department of National Defence with one or two words as to details. It cost $1,400,000 to wash the dirty linen of the Department of National Defence. The navy and air force come a little cheaper than the army, but I suppose that is because one of them lives in the air and the other lives on the water. I am interested in the telephone bill of $911,000 and would be interested in knowing in how many of those cases a letter with airmail and special delivery stamps would not have done just as well. Long distance telephoning is so easy: you just reach for the telephone and you do not have to pay for it yourself. I enjoy doing it, and I think

everyone in this house does also. But somehow or other I am sure that this figure could be reduced a lot.
Telephones, telegrams and other communications cost $6,248,000, although much of that is taken up in the form of leased lines for the air force. These fellows must be very loquacious when they spend over $900,000 on long distance telephone calls.
Another thing I want to stress is this amazing figure of $1,775 million, which is the same as for last year. When I first read that, I could not believe my eyes. Next I thought it must be a misprint. Then I thought that there must be some easy explanation that had not occurred to me. I went around looking for it, but I have decided that there is no such easy explanation. I have decided that what this really means is that there was no estimating in any real sense at all. No one out of a lunatic asylum could believe that, if all the various items were considered separately and added up, they would by some magic produce exactly the same figure as a year ago. I do not think that anyone will argue that.
It seems to me that that is a piece of extraordinary effrontery-I can only call it that- on the part of the department. It means that they were not taking us seriously. But worse than that, what about the Department of Finance? I think it is a worse offence on the part of the Department of Finance than on the part of the Department of National Defence. In effect, what is being said is this: "Do not bother about the House of Commons, this will do for them; they are only the elected members, do not bother about them as they do not matter".
That is the way it seems to me. I wish to remind the house that in spite of all we could do the defence estimates are not going to the estimates committee. I can only hope that when these come before the committee of the whole house in the ordinary way it will not be in the last days of the session but at a time that will permit us to go into these items with some care and get to the bottom of them.
There is one other thing I want to say about the Department of National Defence. It has the most extraordinary faculty of increasing its staff, which increased from 45,718 in 1954 to 53,909 in 1955. That seems to me almost incredible and the only way I can explain it is by reference to the theory which was put forward in the London Economist last autumn with regard to the growth of civil service staff. This is called "Parkinson's Law". Several people have seen
23, 1956	2549
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell it, but I think it is worth putting on the record in part. It begins by saying:
It is a commonplace observation that work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion. Thus, an elderly lady of leisure can spend the entire day in writing and dipatching a postcard to her niece at Bognor Regis. An hour will be spent in finding the postcard, another in hunting for spectacles, half an hour in a search for the address, an hour and a quarter in composition, and twenty minutes in deciding whether or not to take an umbrella when going to the pillarbox in the next street. The total effort which would occupy a busy man for three minutes all told may in this fashion leave another person prostrate after a day of doubt, anxiety and toil.
Granted that work (and especially paper work) is thus elastic in its demands on time, it is manifest that there need be little or no relationship between the work to be done and the size of the staff to which it may be assigned. . . . Politicians and taxpayers have assumed (with occasional phases of doubt) that a rising total in the number of civil servants must reflect a growing volume of work to be done. Cynics, in questioning this belief, have imagined that the multiplication of officials must have left some of them idle or all of them able to work for shorter hours. But this is a matter in which faith and doubt seem equally misplaced.
Then we have an illustration of a case in which one official decides he needs an assistant, but he says he must not have just one assistant because that would mean that that man would argue with him. Therefore he would have to have two assistants, and it finally works out to the point where he needs seven officials. The Economist continues:
Seven officials are now doing what one did before. . . . For these seven make so much work for each other that all are fully occupied and A is actually working harder than ever. An incoming document may well come before each of them in turn. Official E decides that it falls within the province of F, who places a draft reply before C, who amends it drastically before consulting D, who asks G to deal with it . . .
I shall say no more about that, but I come back with confidence to my suggestion that this matter should be dealt with in one way, and one only-by allocating amounts.
I wish to speak only for a moment about trade and the balance of payments. After all, nations, like individuals, cannot live indefinitely beyond their means. The enormous deficit of last year has been much in the public mind but, as I have said, the responsible minister took it very lightly. But we cannot repay trade deficits with optimism alone. I was rather disturbed the other day that the Minister of Finance was apparently making light of our dependence on the United States. This was when he spoke in Port Credit. He went as far as to suggest that we might be able to avoid the effects of a United States depression if one comes. He said:
The time may be coming when we won't suffer the same as they do south of the border.


create the feeling in other people that it has created in me, a feeling of something approaching indignation, that when we think we are sitting so pretty we can ignore the welfare of our fellow citizens-if it creates that feeling-then it may eventually have been worth while.
This government is not primarily concerned about the welfare of the unemployed, about the welfare of the maritimes. They are primarily concerned with so arranging matters that they can win the next election. That is the plain, inescapable truth. Let the unemployed get on as best they can; let the people in the maritimes go on for decades more with insuperable handicaps; let the farmers in the west survey sadly their piles of unsold wheat. But let us get ready for the next election.
I fear I have not been as forceful as I would have liked in speaking for the hundreds of thousands of our fellow citizens who have been and continue to be, in so far as this government is concerned, forgotten men and women. I only wish that I could din my words into the ears of every serious, every generous, every responsible citizen of this country and that I might have the gift to persuade them that it is their duty to rise up and demand action.
Further, just as Abraham Lincoln said that a state could not exist half slave and half free, I would like to stress the fact that a state cannot prosper when an important section of its citizens, men and women of character and capacity, are left with inferior opportunities, with a sense of injustice and frustration. If any word of mine today has the slightest influence in bringing this state of affairs to an end, I shall be happy indeed.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming):
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the budget is empty, negative and partisan; that the government shows no concern over either the serious problems of distressed groups and areas or the growing economic domination of Canada by United States interests; and that these and its other failures demonstrate the government's irresponsibility and unfitness to hold office".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to agree with what the hon. member who has just taken his seat said the other evening about the budget having all the earmarks of a standpat budget marking time until we approach the election of 1957. I imagine that when the next budget is brought down about a year from now it will be a very attractive document. The minister will make a very interesting speech full of promises to the Canadian people and then, since Easter will come

about April 21, the house will probably be dissolved and about the middle of June, say the 17th of June, we shall find ourselves having a general election and a new House of Commons elected. I have no objection to that, of course.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am doing what is my right in a free democracy. I am expressing my own opinion, and in spite of the hon. gentleman's objection to it-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not objecting. I 'am only asking a question.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am going ito express my opinions regardless of the hon. gentlemen who, as the Ottawa Citizen remarked last evening, may belong to the Liberal party but are not liberals. I want to say to the minister that I noticed a very marked difference between the budget this year and the budget last year. Last year the minister reduced certain taxes, particularly the income tax. This year there have only been a few reductions in excise and sales taxes. May I say immediately that, although they only amount to some $12 million, I think all of us welcome them because they effect certain adjustments and so on. I think that relief was needed with regard to the excise and sales taxes so as to bring them into line with what I believe is the policy of the government with regard to equipment for farms and other industries like agriculture.
I also noted that at last something which I have considered to be rather incongruous is going to be removed. I refer to the sales tax on antiques. The government is getting a bit antique itself and perhaps that is the reason that after 20 years the tax on antiques coming into this country is to be removed. As a matter of fact, I think one can commend the government for that.
With respect to the fact that there is no reduction in income tax this year, may I say that I do not know that even the reductions in income tax made last year affected materially an overwhelming part of our population. After all, a very large percentage of the population pay no income tax. They are not affected by any reduction. For the people in the lower brackets we found that the reduction last year, in the case of a married man with two or three children, for example, amounted to a little more than a few cents a week for such a man in what might be called the fairly low-middle bracket. Of
23, 1956	2551
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell course the people in the higher brackets received very substantial reductions.
I want to say to the minister that when next year comes and he has this surplus of $113 million, and if his outline of his expectations for the economy during the present year is borne out by the facts, I rather suspect that he will have far more than $113 million to play with provided he does not bring down what I hope he will bring down, namely, an estimate for a national health plan. I would rather see any surplus that is going to accrue during the current year used in bringing down a comprehensive national health plan, far more comprehensive than the minister has outlined to the committee, because I believe that would be the most beneficial thing that could be done by the government of Canada at this time.
Not only do I believe it is the most beneficial thing that can be done for the people generally but it also will be most beneficial for our old age pensioners. I should like to see them get an increase in their pensions. I hope that sooner or later the government will come around to giving them an increase, but I do not know of anything that would be more beneficial to them than a national health plan.
The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) is not in his seat but I should like to say to him that I think the introduction of such a measure will facilitate immigration into this country, particularly from northwestern Europe. When I was in Britain a year and a half ago I found there was a very general understanding that Canada had no national health plan. When I was there letters were appearing in some of the British papers from immigrants who had come to Canada pointing out that they had done pretty well for the first two or three years, but then a serious illness had attacked one of the family and the medical and hospitalization expenses had not only wiped out all they had been able to save but had put them into debt.
When one considers that in most overseas countries from which we like to get as much immigration into Canada as we can they have quite comprehensive plans, then I say to the government, and particularly to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, that Canada needs such a plan to attract immigrants. I believe that we want immigrants because our country is one that still has wide open spaces with plenty of opportunities for immigrants, far more so than when I came here just over 46 years ago. The future is very bright for those who come here, but today all the progressive countries have social security plans that are quite comprehensive. People who think of coming to this country look for

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell social security measures of the kind they would be giving up in leaving home.
May I say one other thing to the minister in this connection. I should like to see the countries of the commonwealth at least try to arrange their social security plans so that people moving from one commonwealth country to another would not lose any benefits. I am thinking particularly, of course, of the old age pensioners. Incidentally, today our old age pensions are on a contribution basis as old age pensions are in the United Kingdom. Our old age pensioners have made a special contribution of 2 per cent through the sales tax and consequently they have paid a premium. They should be entitled to their old age pension no matter where they may be, no matter whether a pensioner moves to Great Britain perhaps to stay with a younger sister after spending 30 or 40 years in Canada.
I have in mind at the moment a lady some 76 years old who is going to Britain to visit a younger sister. She must be back within three months. Yet I know perfectly well she could be cared for better over there provided she could get the old age pension in the same way that old age pensions are paid by some countries regardless of residence. So then I hope if the minister has a substantial surplus next year, that surplus will be used not to reduce corporation taxes, not even to reduce income taxes, but rather to bring our social security system up to the level it should be in order to give our people the kind of security they need and make the country more attractive to the kind of immigrants we want to get.
Then, too, I want to say to the minister that whether we have a surplus or not I would hope that we might use more of our revenue for the projects of the United Nations and our own Colombo plan, to assist in raising the standards of living across the world. On two occasions during the past week I have heard two competent observers who have been in the Soviet union. I heard Mr. Norman Smith on Tuesday evening, and he illustrated his lecture with pictures he had taken, mainly in Moscow. On Wednesday, of course, I listened to Mr. James Duncan of the Massey-Harris-Ferguson company. While listening to both of these addresses I realized what the challenge is that we are facing anew in the world today. Here we face a powerfully organized country. It is true it is dominated by a very small group of men and does not have the democratic procedures that we have. They are improving their output of material things every year and are now offering to assist the more underprivileged peoples of the world. These people who do not understand


what democracy means will, I think, be influenced by those who can assist them most rapidly in emerging from their underprivileged position. I think we have to do a lot more than we have been doing in support of the United Nations technical aid and the Colombo plan. As I suggested to the minister of external affairs the other day, we should give our support to the special United Nations fund for economic development which is known as SUNFED.
May I also add that another thing that impressed me in connection with these two lectures was the tremendous urge and the tremendous planning of educational activities in the Soviet Union. In spite of the dictatorship, its cruelty and all the rest of it-which I hope has now passed but I am not yet convinced of that-the extent to which the old Russian culture has been encouraged and brought up to date has been impressive. I was not here yesterday when there was some discussion about pictures for the national gallery. I want to tell the minister that so far as I am concerned I believe we are not doing enough in the way of encouraging culture in this country. I think when we acquire good art and have a proper national gallery in which to put that art, we are doing something of inestimable value for the future of our country. I am not going to enter into a debate as to whether or not commissions should be paid for buying those pictures, but I am very happy indeed to know the national gallery is acquiring some first class pictures, because to say that man does not live by bread alone is as true today as it was when it was said long years ago.
This brings me to the proposal in the budget to place a 20 per cent excise tax on certain magazines that are published in the United States, or elsewhere, I presume, and are brought into this country in which advertising is invited from Canadian advertisers. I am in complete sympathy with the object of that particular tax, but I am very doubtful as to its efficacy. I doubt very much that the 20 per cent excise tax will do anything substantial towards discontinuing the publication of those magazines in this country. What I think may happen is that the advertising rates may be increased by 20 per cent. If the circulation of Time and Reader's Digest is sufficiently attractive to the advertisers, we shall not achieve the objective the minister has in mind. I want to assure him, however, that I am in complete sympathy with the objective of the proposal.
I think a more positive approach would be to set up the Canada Council to carry out some of the recommendations that are found in the Massey report. I am not narrowing that

down to magazines, literature and so on, but I am thinking of the need for expansion in the field of education and for the building up of our educational facilities. I was impressed the other evening when I heard of the great university in Moscow, the thousands of students that are there and the numbers of highly qualified engineers and technical men that are being turned out, and I realized that our own universities have had to cut down on the number of students that they can accommodate. They have had to raise certain standards in order to keep students out. Now, those standards are not always the standards that are desirable. The fact that a student is proficient in one field on an examination paper and is not as proficient in another field may limit that student's right to enter a university. I know, both from my experience as a teacher and my experience as a student in the old days-I am not going to make any confessions-that there were one or two subjects I not only found very difficult but only as the result of considerable cramming did I manage to get the 52 per cent or 53 per cent that was required to put me through. Yet I am quite sure that in other fields I was fairly proficient. So, I think we have to pay much more attention to the recommendations in the Massey report. I believe the minister will have to provide from time to time, not only grants in aid to our universities but grants for the provision of scholarships for young Canadians who have the ability and the desire to go on with education.
Again may I point out that it is the boast in Britain today that no child with ability need be denied a university education if that child and the parents of that child desire the education. Through systems of bursaries, scholarships and nominations, today every child in the United Kingdom can attain a higher education. We have not reached that stage in Canada. I think probably the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) was right the other evening when he said we could look into our defence expenditures a little more closely. I would not like to rise in this house and move a motion to reduce defence expenditures under this budget by $200 million or $300 million. Yet in my own mind I am convinced that if this department were gone into very carefully, $200 million, $300 million, $400 million or even $500 million might be saved. Of course, you might have to spend it in certain other defence projects under circumstances that might arise. I do not know, but I am quite sure that there are unnecessary expenditures and extravagances that could be dealt with.
I listened to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) this morning when
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell he talked about the encouragement of private enterprise. Well, I think there are some fields in which private enterprise can serve the nation. But when I hear criticisms, following a plea for private enterprise, of the manner in which, for example, the United States corporations and investors are entering the Canadian economy, I sometimes wonder what those who criticize the lack of encouragement of private enterprise have in mind, because if we are to have complete private enterprise, let us have it. If we have complete private enterprise, then there should be no let or hindrance of any person or any corporation coming into our economy and making out of it the best that he or it can possibly get out of it. I cannot go along with the idea that if we get rid of some of our enterprises that because of their very nature have to be public enterprise we would be performing any service to this country.
I noted the reference to the Trans-Canada Air Lines, a very efficient airway system, and I also saw-I have not got it with me; if I had known it was coming up this morning I might have had it-the figures that have been published regarding air traffic. The number of passengers carried between great cities like Chicago and New York and in our own country, although very much less impressive, if divided between two transcontinental air lines, would mean that neither of them could pay expenses. Therefore, we have to be careful when we talk of encouraging private enterprise to define what that encouragement should be, and how it should be undertaken.
As far as we are concerned, we criticize the alienation of our resources to foreign corporations because we believe that we should be planning the development of those resources ourselves. If we have to, why are all these things not public enterprises? I voted for a resolution introduced by the official opposition a short time ago. In the resolution the official opposition urged that the federal authority and the provinces should co-operate in the development of our resources. How? Well, as far as we are concerned we think that should be undertaken very largely by public enterprise because private enterprise has failed to do the job.
Those are some of the things that struck me. I say to the minister, I noted that he admitted in his speech that some sectors of industry and agriculture have not fully shared in the rate of progress which he outlined in his speech. He said there was some unevenness in the rate of expansion; and, of course, this implies that the condition of agriculture has been improving. As a matter of fact there was some improvement in

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell agricultural returns in 1955 over 1954, but nothing commensurate with the need of agriculture. Agriculture has been steadily losing ground over the last number of years. For example, last year corporation profits climbed by almost 30 per cent in the first three quarters-I have not the figure for the fourth quarter'-as compared with the same period in 1954; but net farm income fell in the same period from $2,155 million in 1951 to $1,126 million in 1954, a decline of 47-8 per cent. But, as I said a moment ago, there was some improvement last year. However, 10 per cent or so increase in improvement last year will not compensate for the nearly 48 per cent decline in the period which I mentioned a moment ago.
Then, of course, we are all happy that we have not unemployment to the extent this year that we had a year ago, but there is still a considerable amount of unemployment, or at least there are large numbers of people who are seeking jobs. The last figure which I have seen indicates that there were 515,000 unplaced applicants. I will say immediately that they are not all unemployed, but they are unplaced applicants for jobs as at February 16 of this year. It is true that that is a better figure than the figure of a year ago, which I think was in the neighbourhood of 600,000; but it still indicates a very serious condition in the field of employment. It does not matter whether he is one in 100,000 men, 400,000 men or 500,000, it does not matter how many there are, the person who is unemployed suffers whether he is accompanied by a very large number or a very few people. Anyone who has had the experience of standing in a relief line, asking for a meal ticket and then going away and getting a meal on a meal ticket will know what it does to one. I did that once, not because I was unemployed but because I wanted to see what the treatment was, and I found it very much to my consternation. Fortunately, since those days-I refer to 1921-we have introduced unemployment insurance and we have other means to .assist the unemployed; but still there are those who suffer in the manner in which they suffered in 1921, a smaller number perhaps, but yet nonetheless the suffering is there.
I cannot deal with all the matters that I had in mind when I was thinking of what I would say in connection with this debate. But I do want to say to the minister that he still has in his budget and in his methods of collection of taxes tremendous loopholes which should be plugged. In the legislation there are loopholes under which rich and powerful corporations in many fields, and well-to-do individuals in those fields, can in various ways evade what I think is their fair


share of the burden of financing the public business of this country. We believe that ability to pay is of course fundamental and upon which we should base all our taxation. I think there is no fairer method of taxation than income tax, and it has the other saving grace that the person who pays the income tax knows that he is paying and contributing to the country. I am going to give the example that I have given before, and nothing that the minister or his predecessor has said has changed my opinion that it is wrong. At the present time a man can receive some $14,000 in a given year from dividends and so on and pay no income tax. A man with $3,000, if he has no children, will pay $150 income tax. The man with $14,000, similarly married with no children, if his income is derived, as I said, from dividends from a Canadian mining, oil or gas company, pays only his old age security tax of $60 and nothing more.
I would like to put on the record the method by which I worked that out in order that the minister and others in the house can see how it is arrived at and if they wish to try to explain it or criticize it they may do so. I took an actual amount because it comes out evenly. I used the case of a man with an income of $14,542 derived as I have just indicated. If we deduct tax exemptions of $2,000 for the taxpayer and his wife, that gives us a total deduction of $2,000. I then deducted 20 per cent depletion allowance, which is $2,908 and leaves a taxable income of $9,634. The old age security tax is, of course, $60. Income tax other than old age security tax is $1,957. The tax on investment income, which is 4 per cent on $9,237, gives $369. Tax payable before tax credit, that is apart from old age security tax, is $2,326. The taxpayer gets a tax credit of 20 per cent of $11,634, or $2,327. In other words, not only does he pay no tax but he has one dollar left over to come and go on. Of course, I took into account 20 per cent on income from dividends after depletion allowances are deducted.
I think that system should be changed. I think it is an injustice. It means there is a tax exemption of almost $14,000 for one couple and an exemption of only $2,000 for another. When a person who derives his income from dividends begins to pay income tax at all over and above the $14,000 he begins at a rate of 9-6 per cent instead of 15 per cent as in the case of the man who works for his money and who makes only $3,000. That is not fair and of course it has a fantastic result.
I could go on and deal at further length with this question but there is one other matter with which I want to deal and that is

the depletion allowance itself. I have only a few minutes in which to deal with this subject. Depletion allowances have become extremely important in our structure. Depletion allowances eliminate from corporation taxes 33J *per cent of profits in the case of oil and gas companies, companies operating base and precious metal mines and industrial mineral mines. Coal mine owners have a depletion allowance of ten cents per ton. In the case of oil and gas and mining companies this means that up to one-third of the public's share in our natural resources, and I regard them as such, is given back as a massive subsidy to those who are exploiting those resources.
I am not the only person criticizing the depletion allowances. We have another example in Professor F. E. La Brie, who, in his book "Introduction to Income Tax Law- Canada", published last year, wrote:
A deduction for depletion that is not limited to capital cost not only permits taxpayers to recoup capital expenditure tax-free but permits them to realize tax-free capital gain through an incomeearning process of exploitation.
"A" spends $100,000 in discovering an oil well. The potential yield of the oil well is $3 million. "A" through a depletion allowance of 331 per cent, may take $1 million worth of oil from the well tax-free. Does this not permit him a tax-free capital gain of $900,000?
I think it does. I think the answer is in the affirmative in the example which Professor La Brie gives. These depletion allowances are altogether out of line today and we should plug the hole and institute a capital gains tax in order that the country may receive something from these great inflated values which are often created.
I wish to cite another recent example before I conclude. On March 17 I read about Algoma Steel Corporation whose profits, according to the latest consolidated statement, were $10,400,000 in 1955 compared with $4,500,000 last year. The thing I particularly noticed was that stock exchange quotations on Algoma have climbed from $49 a share in January, 1954, to $121 as at March 15 of this year. What of the man who bought a thousand shares of Algoma something over two years ago? He makes an income of over $70,000, or a capital gain if you like, just for sitting and watching the ticker-tape in a broker's office, and yet this is tax-free and can be used as income.
I could give another and more striking example but I do not have time to do so today. I imagine it is deals of this description, however, which account for many of the new cars we see in such large quantities. I cannot understand how people with incomes ranging from $6,000 to $8,000 a year can buy new cars each year. We speak of inflation. One of the ways by which we could 67509-162
The Budget-Mr. Blackmofe stop this tremendous demand would be to put on a capital gains tax. The minister may say that it is difficult to do and I agree that this is so. It is difficult to know what capital gains should be taxed but I think that difficulty can be overcome. I believe that the people who are making large incomes by manipulation and speculation on the stock market should be called upon to pay part of their gains to the government and the people of Canada whose resources are the basis of exploitation and speculation.
I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis):
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein immediately after the words "United States interests" the following words:
"that it has failed to reduce the burden of sales and income taxes on those in the lower income groups, while continuing to favour privileged interests and those with unearned incomes by maintaining the 20 per cent dividend tax credit and by refusing to impose a tax on capital gains."
The amendment as amended would then read:
This house regrets that the budget is empty, negative and partisan; that the government shows no concern over either the serious problems of distressed groups and areas or the growing economic domination of Canada by United States interests; that it has failed to reduce the burden of sales and income taxes on those in the lower income groups, while continuing to favour privileged interests and those with unearned incomes by maintaining the 20 per cent dividend tax credit and by refusing to impose a tax on capital gains; and that these and its other failures demonstrated the government's irresponsibility and unfitness to hold office.
At one o'clock the house took recess.
