Mr. Speaker, because of the unfortunate absence of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and because of the fact that the Social Credit group in this house have conferred upon me the responsibility and privilege of being the chairman of the banking and commerce committee representing the Social Credit group, it becomes my duty to speak in relation to the budget speech which the Minister of Finance delivered in this house on the evening of March 20.
Before proceeding may I ask the Minister of Finance whether or not he believes that in Canada what is physically possible ought to be financially possible. I do not expect the minister to answer that, but I suggest that during the remarks which I shall make, he keep his mind concentrated on that question and on the marvellous physical capacities of Canada.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend wants an answer, I have a firm belief that the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament are competent to do a great many things. I would not want to say that within the realm of human activity nothing is impossible.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad the minister made that reply. He was straightforward and honest just as he is in everything else. I must say that he has committed himself to a considerable proposition. It is well that he said that, before I go forward now with what I have to say. I should like to quote from page 771 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the House of Commons banking and commerce committee for 1939. Mr. Jaques asked Mr. Towers, then president of the Bank of Canada, this question and received this answer:
Q. Would you admit that anything physically possible and desirable can be made financially possible?
A. Certainly.
No qualification to the answer at all. Under those circumstances I have the idea that we are justified in being a bit exacting in respect of the minister with regard to this budget speech. I have noticed that many newspaper reports throughout Canada have expressed disappointment relative to the budget, and some of them have expressed rather strong disapproval.
The minister is an honourable, conscientious and able man and he has to assist him in his department a staff of what should be highly trained and honourable, conscientious and able men. People in this house and in Canada generally are warranted in assuming that the minister and his department have produced what they conscientiously believe to be the best budget which could be produced for the year 1956 considering the many and varied circumstances confronting Canada.
If there are in the present budget unjustifiable deficiencies, as many people including Social Crediters think there are, then it is well that we ask ourselves who is to blame for those deficiencies. I have not seen one newspaper in Canada asking that question, not one. That is a remarkable thing. Is the minister to blame? Are his departmental advisers to blame? Or is the orthodox financial system to blame, the financial system under which the minister operates, the financial system under whose tenets the minister and the department and the government have been under the necessity of managing, or have thought they were?
What are some of the basic deficiencies in this budget? To help ourselves to more satisfactorily judge, may we ask ourselves,

and try to arrive at the answers to, certain fundamental questions. They are simple, almost childishly easy to answer. First, what is a financial system? Second, what are the functions which a financial system should perform? What have we in Canada the right to expect the Department of Finance under the minister's direction to do for Canada? Third, what is an economic system? Fourth, what are the functions that an economic system should perform?
May we answer those questions. Answering question No. 1, it might be said with a considerable degree of accuracy that the financial system of a community is the system by means of which that community provides money for the use of the community as a whole and as individuals. Answering question No. 2, it might be said that the functions of a community's financial system are three, namely, first, to defray the expenses of carrying on the work of governing the community; second, to render available to would-be producers the loans they need with which to produce adequate goods and services for the community; and third, to render available to the members of the community-I imagine a number will object to this one although it is unanswerable and inevitable-the money necessary to enable them to consume what they need, or their full equitable share of, the community's production. This is the point which Social Crediters particularly stress.
Expressing the answer in another way, we might with accuracy say that the function of a community's financial system is to make financially possible for the community and its members what is physically possible and desirable in the community, having regard to the community's resources, material and human.
Answering question No. 3, it might be said that a community's economic system is the system by means of which the community, either as a whole or as individuals, produces or produce goods and services and delivers or deliver and distributes or distribute those goods and services, either for consumption within the community or for exchange or trade with other communities for goods and services for consumption in the community. I think there will be hardly any argument regarding the answers I have given thus far.
Answering question No. 4, it might be said that the basic and essential functions of an economic system are to produce and to deliver goods and services, as required, when required and where required; and that the two incidental functions performed in the process of production are, first, to distribute among the consumers more or less the purchasing power with which those consumers

may buy and consume a portion of the products of the community and, second, to provide employment and jobs to members of the community from which they get purchasing power with which to obtain and consume a portion of the products of the community.
Many people go astray in their thinking in respect of these last two points which I have made. There are a good many people who think that unless business, unless the factories, unless the mercantile institutions, unless firms and other productive enterprises can hire all the people in the community, then those enterprises are failing in their functions. This is a serious fallacy.
Many people, and I fear most of my Liberal and Conservative friends are included, believe that as an industry such as a coal mine or a textile mill produces coal or textiles, it puts into the hands of the people enough money with which to buy that coal or those textiles. This is a complete and utter fallacy which leads the country far astray in its effort to think its way through the difficult economic situations that prevail and confront us.
Now I go on to another matter which indicates how responsible the minister before us is. The finance department controls the financial system and the economic system. The finance department in the government of a community is the department that directly controls and manages the financial system of the community and that at the same time indirectly controls and manages the community's economic system, since in our time, sustained production of goods is impossible without money, or at least credit, which is another form of money. Before long we will have the minister carrying plenty of responsibility. The community's minister of finance is therefore, in effect, likewise the community's economic minister, so that we are justified in saying the Minister of Finance is the minister of finance and economics.
The Minister of Finance, in his twofold capacity as Canada's minister of finance and economics, is responsible to this house and to the Canadian nation to see that, first, money is provided for defraying the expenses of governing Canada, as I said before; second, money is made available to Canadian producers and would-be producers adequately to enable them to produce whatever kinds and quantities of goods are necessary to provide all Canadians with abundant living, in so far as Canadian resources, material and human, permit.
I think: everyone in this house and in the country agrees that the resources of this country are such, and that the industrial equipment of this country is such, and that 67509-162J

The Budget-Mr. Blackmoi'e the transportation facilities and communication facilities of this country are such, and the human beings in this country are such, that there is no excuse whatsoever for this country producing anything short of abundant living for every person in Canada. If it is failing to do that, whose responsibility is it? It must be the Minister of Finance's responsibility, for he is the minister of the financial system and the economic system, as I pointed out.
Now we have a basis on which we can begin to criticize scientifically and intelligently the budget that has been placed before us. Criticisms of the budget commonly heard are so vague and rambling and piecemeal that it makes a person almost weary to think that that is the best people know what to say about a budget.
I have said it is the minister's business to make money available for two purposes: first of all, to run the country and, second, to provide money for producers so that they can get the money. The third responsibility is to provide money or make it available to all Canadians adequately to enable them to buy and consume the desirable goods which Canadians produce. If this is not so, then it makes no difference how much milk, cream, butter, cheese, fruit and other products the people of Canada produce, it will be impossible for the people of Canada to buy and consume them. Consequently, it is conceivable that people can be going in great misery in the presence of the most astounding abundance throughout the land. Here I believe is where the Social Crediters and other members of the house part company. If any member can find a flaw in that reasoning let him get up when the opportunity comes and point out the flaw and establish his case. I defy him to do it.
All of this means that in effect the Minister of Finance is responsible for seeing that money is made available for providing markets for Canadian producers. Generally the common talk about markets is so vague, inconsistent and unreasonable that we get nowhere. Few people seem to realize that in a country like this we can produce our own markets within our own country for all the goods our people are able to use. The person whose responsibility it is to produce those markets is the Minister of Finance. Has be done it? We can see now where we are approaching real deficiencies in the budget.
A fourth responsibility of the minister is to make money available, by reason of the foregoing, so that whatever is physically possible is financially possible, having regard to Canadian resources, material and human, as I have indicated by the passage I read not long ago from Mr. Graham Towers. When

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore Mr. Graham Towers was before the banking and commerce committee in 1939, he was honest and frank, he certainly knew his business, but he got so cagey after a few years that he did not dare to commit himself on anything. But you may be sure that what Graham Towers told us in those early days was fact, for when he took over he was qualified for his job.
I now turn to the budget speech, having referred to these standards by which to judge the budget speech. The budget speech is, or ought to be, in effect the minister's annual report in respect of the discharge of his responsibilities in relation to the functions of his department, both as Minister of Finance and as minister of economics, that is, as minister of production of goods and as minister of markets for goods.
Let us examine the budget speech, the report of the minister's performance. Has the minister performed these functions as Canadians have a full right to expect those functions to be performed? Before I say anything more, I suggest we give that matter a few moment's thought. Looking at the budget from this point of view, what are some of the deficiencies quickly discoverable? Let us review the minister's full responsibilities as to providing money, and see whether or not he has adequately discharged all those during the year 1955-56 and is prepared to discharge them in 1956-57.
Having regard to Canada's resources, has the minister been able to discharge his number one responsibility, namely, to provide the money to defray the expenses that ought to be incurred in carrying on the work of governing Canada? I believe that I cannot be successfully challenged when I say that except perhaps in the case of the Department of National Revenue alone, there is not one single department in the present government that has anything like the amount of money it needs and could spend without causing inflation, if only the minister could get the money. Now, he knows how true that all is.
Let us concentrate on the question of getting the money and leave aside all the foolish talk we often hear in the newspapers and elsewhere. He knows very well that there is not a department in the government that has not asked for much more money than he was able to give, and he knows they could use it.
Take, for example, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Think what the minister, energetic, able and idealistic and ambitious, could do in respect of our parks alone, if he just had the money. Think what a wonderland this country would be as an attraction to tourists, and how
[Mr. Blackmore.l

rapidly we would begin to do away with our adverse trade balance with the United States. But the minister is hampered and cramped in every direction because he just has not the money. That indicates that the Minister of Finance has fallen down with respect to that department.

I will come to that in due time. All things in season. Take the Department of National Defence. Nothing need be said in regard to money required for that department. The Minister of National Defence could probably use four times the amount of money he has at his disposal in respect of the Department of National Defence, and he has had to be limited by the Minister of Finance because the latter has said, "I cannot get the money." He has not told him whether or not the goods and the resources and the people of Canada can build the kind of organization that the Minister of National Defence wants. He just said, "I cannot get the money." Why could he not get the money? If what is physically possible can be made financially possible, then unquestionably the minister stands condemned for deficiency in performance with respect to the administration of the Department of National Defence.
Take health and welfare. Think what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) would do if he had plenty of money in respect of civil defence, which we all know we need, old age pensions, health insurance and all that sort of thing. You can just imagine what a happy land he would soon make this country if he only just had the money. He has all the human and material resources available. There is all the material in Canada necessary to build every hospital he wants. There are all the people necessary to train nurses and doctors and give every kind of service which is necessary in our hospitals. All the goods and services and the capacity to produce such are here to produce the perfect set-up for national health.

Let me finish my speech and then ask your questions. I shall be glad to answer them all. Otherwise we just cannot go ahead in a straightforward manner.
I have already put questions to the hon. member and other hon. members. If he can answer them let him take the floor when I am finished. Take transport. We have not got it done yet and we will talk for weeks and weeks about

Mr. Speaker, last year after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) had ended his budget speech, a whole series of opposition speakers, particularly Progressive Conservative members, rose to express their concern and complaints about increasing unemployment in this country. While expressing these fears the members of the opposition indicated that unrest was on the way. Deep in their hearts, though, they were happy over this state of affairs since they believed that some political advantage could be reaped from it.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) admitted that with five and a half million workers in this country, there could very well be some falling off in employment. He added, however, that this was only temporary and, along with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) went on to state that there would be an improvement in the economy and in the labour situation. Everything came out as had been predicted by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Prosperity in this country in 1955 to 1956 was all but unexampled in the post war period. But it will be nothing compared to the prosperity we will enjoy in 1956. In fact Canadian industry throughout this country will have a greatly increased payroll to distribute amongst our working people. Workers' wages will go up because this boom will especially benefit the workers.

The Liberal party has but one concern, that of fattening this pay envelope year after year, and it is happy about it. Besides, the government should have no greater concern than this desire for greater prosperity in Canada, for well it knows that the workers are the ones who benefit most from it. This prosperity, which is a government responsibility, is far more important than the lowering of taxes even though, of course, everybody, myself included, would like them to be lower. In 1956, an amount of 12 to 13 billion dollars will be paid in salaries to the people of Canada. It should not be overlooked also that the Liberal party, which enacted social legislation for the people of this country, does not hesitate to expand this field of social legislation, family allowances, pensions, insurance of all kinds and so on. We are probably the most advanced people in the world, considering the ratio of population, in this field of social legislation. This year again, further benefits have been offered.
We want to go even further by offering you health insurance which will be particularly beneficial to the poor people of our country. Henceforth, through that legislation, the poor will be able to receive the same treatment as the rich as far as health services are concerned.

These new proposals are embodied in rather complicated formulas, upon which the minister did not enlarge at any length. These formulas are given at page 2328 of Hansard and I will not repeat them here. However, I wish to point out that the federal government is satisfied since the minister says so at page 2316 of Hansard:
Under all the circumstances we believe our offer is eminently fair and it is reasonable and realistic in the light of federal and provincial responsibilities.
However, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the provinces are not dancing to the same tune; in fact, I believe that their reaction is directly the opposite. As far as I know, no provincial premier has been able, upon leaving Ottawa in February, to tell the same thing as the Minister of Finance, that is:
Under all the circumstances we believe our offer is eminently fair and it is reasonable and realistic in the light of federal and provincial responsibilities.
I do not think that any provincial premier made a statement along the same lines. The statements issued since that time are unequivocal particularly the one made recently by the premier of Ontario (Mr. Frost), the day following the budget speech. "Ontario, he said, did not get a single cent out of the new proposals. We complain, but' Ottawa is playing deaf. We want to assume our responsibility, we ask for nothing new that does not belong to us. As I say, Ontario is only seeking to get a reasonable share of the tax fields granted

our province by the constitution." Since that conference was held, I believe that each of the premiers of the provinces of Canada has made a similar statement.
Mr. Speaker, the new proposals offer no solution at all in the matter of tax centralization, and as Canada keeps growing this is bearing more and more heavily on the provinces.
The development of our country imposes on provincial governments very heavy responsibilities which they have to meet under the constitution.
I would even say that the development of this country burdens the provinces with additional expenses while the benefits of our present fiscal system accrue to the federal government, since the amount of the budget is geared to the amount of the national income.
Mr. Speaker, sections 92 and 93 of the constitution, which it is well to recall from time to time, list the powers held exclusively by the provinces and the fields which are the responsibility of provincial legislatures. The ones concerning us as regards expenses are listed in paragraphs 6, 7 and 8. Paragraph 6 includes:
The establishment, maintenance, and management of public and reformatory prisons in and for, the province:
7.	The establishment, maintenance, and management of hospitals, asylums, charities, and eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals;
8.	Municipal institutions in the province;
And the tenth paragraph includes:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes.
Then there is mention of public works within the limits of a province, highway construction in general, in short, all public works.
Section 93 gives provinces exclusive powers in the matter of education. Each province passes its own legislation concerning education. Add to that social legislation within the jurisdiction of the provinces. There we have an idea of the heavy obligations carried by provincial legislatures.
It is undeniable, Mr. Speaker, that the development of this country involves financial burdens for the provinces. Who will deny the urgent and heavy needs of education at all levels: universities, high schools, technical schools, primary schools, in all provinces? According to experts and to ministers responsible for education in all provinces, these burdens will increase further in the future and will become greater according to needs.

Provinces have the duty and the responsibility of providing for universities, technical schools, school boards and secondary schools. An examination of the financial statement of those institutions shows that their needs are urgent.
The same thing applies to municipal corporations. Most of those corporations, not to say all of them, are badly in need of health and social welfare services.
They must provide waterworks, sewers, sidewalks, streets, establish fire-fighting services and so forth. All those works are urgently needed as a result of the rapid development of cities and towns. The state of imbalance of municipal budgets shows that corporations are absolutely unable to cope even with essential works.
The same situation prevails in the provincial field of highways, public health, school legislation and public works. Each of the Canadian provinces cannot cope with essential needs because legislatures do not have sufficient revenues and they would not be able to do more as a result of the new offers now made by the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian constitution gave the provinces the power to legislate in the field of direct taxation in order that they may have sufficient revenues to fulfil their obligations. Paragraph 2, section 92 of the British North America Act states that in each province the legislature has the exclusive right of legislating in matters of direct taxation within the limits of the province in order to raise the necessary revenue for provincial purposes. That section, Mr. Speaker, still appears in our constitution.
In 1942, in order to meet the needs of national defence, the federal government laid its hands on the provincial taxation powers but only after having undertaken to return such rights to the provinces at the end of the war. Eleven years later, after many conferences and bargaining sessions, the provinces have managed to recover a small part of what is rightfully theirs.
With the money obtained from provincial sources of revenue, the federal government has handed back a few millions in the overbearing manner of a millionaire throwing a few crumbs. This fiscal centralization allows the government to accumulate sums of five billions of dollars a year, an invitation to waste and extravagance as has been shown by the Currie investigation and the more recent evidence of retired officers. This hap-
23, 1956	2567
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron pens when all other levels of government, provincial, municipal or educational, can barely get by and have not enough revenue to meet their needs.
There is enough taxation money in Canada to meet all needs. The taxpayer is bled to the limit on account of that centralization. It is a problem of distribution resulting from the fact that neither the spirit nor the letter of the Canadian constitution has been respected.
The budget brings no remedy. Inevitably this will lead, one day or another, to disastrous consequences for the federal system on which Canadian politics is based.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative amendment to this motion, I think, puts its finger on one of the oddities of this budget which has been presented and of the address given to us by the Minister of Finance. It was an address and a budget presentation singularly devoid of information. In fact, I begin to wonder whether in future we may expect to have
2568	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron budget speeches as empty of content as the speeches from more august sources to which we have become accustomed, speeches that conceal more than they reveal.
However, the Minister of Finance did give us more information in another place, in the papers he tabled a day or two before the presentation of the budget. In those papers one can glean one piece of information that gives one some idea of just what is taking place in the Canadian economy at this time, the economy the minister referred to as so buoyant and optimistic.
I am always interested in the people behind the statistics. Sometimes we tend to lump human beings into columns of figures and call them so many of this and so many of that. I like to find out what is going on with the people themselves when we look behind the figures. On page 11 of the papers tabled by the Minister of Finance I find this:
In 1955	.	.	. improved business conditions
brought about a large increase in labour income and there was at the same time a substantial recovery in net farm income because of a better western grain crop. These were the major factors in the increase of $1,593 million or 9 per cent in total personal income. Labour income, which is by far the largest element in personal income, rose by $872 million or 7 per cent, and accounted for 55 per cent of the total increase.
When we read that, we feel that the ordinary Canadian citizen is probably doing fairly well with the buoyant economy which the minister boasts is actually here. But then when we turn back in the same document to page 6, we find some other information that reveals that there were other people in our economy who were doing very much better than those categorized as labour or farm. We find on page 6 the following:
In 1955 investment income increased by $756 million or by about one-fifth, and reached a total of $4,471 million.
There is rather a striking contrast between the increase of 7 per cent that was added to labour income and the increase of 20 per cent that was added to investment income. It is particularly striking in view of the fact that it does not actually reveal the whole of the tribute levied on the economy of Canada by those who own the means of wealth production, because I discovered this. Not only was there an additional $756 million distributed by way of dividends, rent and other forms of investment income, but I also find that there was a tremendous amount of money left in undistributed profits to Canadian corporations, amounting as a matter of fact to almost a billion dollars, $913 million which, in addi-


tion to the dividends distributed, amounting to some $727 million, makes a grand total of $1,640 million that went to the owners of corporation shares in Canada.
That does not tell the whole of the story, because the Minister of Finance tells us on page 14 of his white paper of certain other emoluments accruing to business, and he points out that business saving is composed of two principal items, depreciation allowances and undistributed profits. I have already pointed out that in 1955 undistributed profits amounted to $913 million, and I also find that there was some $206 million in depreciation allowances.
It is true enough that part of depreciation allowances can, I suppose, correctly be classified as depreciation costs. They do actually go to replace worn-out capital goods. But the very fact that the minister describes depreciation allowances and lumps them with undistributed profits as part of savings indicates what, of course, most of us have always known, that a very considerable part of what we know as depreciation allowances are in actual fact hidden and undisclosed profits.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there is something a little odd about an economy which distributes its wealth in the way in which we do in Canada. I consulted the taxation statistics published in 1955 and based on the figures for 1953, and I found that those who are classified as being in receipt of investment income constitute only 5-75 per cent of the total of our taxpayers. When we take into account the fact that the taxpayers of Canada only constitute a proportion of the adult population, then we can see what a very small proportion of our population is receiving this enormous sum of money each year which accrues in the form of dividends, undistributed profits and depreciation allowances. They are only 5-75 of the total of income taxpayers, and they number some 62,320 people which, if one consults the census figures and the dominion bureau of statistics figures, one will find amounts to about 1 per cent of the heads of Canadian families. One per cent of the heads of Canadian families were in receipt of nearly $2,000 million in 1955.
Let us compare that with those who are receiving labour income, which was classified by the minister as the largest item of personal income. According to the taxation statistics, employees constitute 73-14 per cent of the total of income taxpayers. We have to remember that there are a great many people who not only are not in the 5-75 per cent of taxpayers who draw investment income but are not in the 73-14 per cent of taxpayers who constitute the labour force employees of

the country. There are a great many employees in the country who do not reach that category at all, which makes the proportion of those who are in receipt of investment income even more strikingly small.
Just what have we been doing with regard to this distribution of wealth in Canada? There are some very interesting figures to be gleaned from dominion bureau of statistics publications. I find, for instance, that it is estimated that in 1955 the amount of corporation taxes accruing to the treasury was some 17 per cent more than it had been in the previous year, 1954. I find also that the increase in corporation profits in that same year was 24 per cent. Most striking of all, Mr. Speaker, I find that the increase in profits after taxation was no less than 30 per cent.
When we are faced with this situation it is extremely difficult to understand the government's determined maintenance of the scandalous tax exemption accorded to investment income in this country. I know that the traditional and classical explanation of it is that we require to encourage savings in order to promote investment and thereby develop our economy. But I suggest to you, sir, that when the corporations of this country put aside $913 million in the form of undistributed profits and when in addition, due to the generosity of the government, they are also able to tuck away another $206 million in depreciation allowances, we do not need to worry very much about making sure that the people who are drawing investment money are going to have some savings in order to reinvest them.
I suggest that the situation we have to face is this. While there are 62,000 odd in receipt of investment income, among those 62,000 there will be many thousands whose personal share will be extremely small, a matter of $100 or $200 a year, if that much, and they are all lumped in with the 62,000. I suggest, sir, that if we could only find out just how much each one of the 62,000 was getting we would be able to narrow this down to a minute group of our population in control of this vast sum of savings that accumulate from the processes of industry.
Not only that, sir, but we have had plain evidence for some time past, and it has been stressed again and again in the house this session and mentioned outside the house, that the investment policy of those who now control the pools of wealth in this country is highly unsatisfactory both to financial and to political leaders. I suggest, sir, that we might do well to consider placing more in the hands of the ordinary Canadian citizen rather than continuing to place it in the hands of those people who are apparently reluctant to use the privileged position we have given
23. 1956	2569
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron them for any consistent policy of development in this country, with the consequence that we hear on all sides, we heard it again today, cries of distress because of the influx of United States capital taking over the riskier and more adventurous types of development in Canada.
I suggest to you, sir, that not only is there something very unhealthy in giving special privileges to this already extremely privileged group, but there is something very dangerous about it too. While it is true that the increase in investment income did not quite reach the increase in wage and salary income, it came very close to it, and while it did not quite reach it, nevertheless the increase in wages and salaries does indicate a very serious situation in our economy when compared with the increase in investment income and the increase in undistributed corporate profits.
I do not think we need be surprised that this is the case. We have had evidence that there is something quite unhealthy in our economy. This session we have had some more strong evidence of it, because I cannot consider any society healthy in which there is a profitable field for loan companies' to lend at 24 per cent to enable people to pay their bills. There is something radically unsound in our methods of wealth distribution in this country. In fact I believe, Mr. Speaker, we could perhaps draw an analogy from the natural world. We all know that when the prospective victim shows signs of sickness and failing, the vultures appear. The vultures are appearing in great numbers on our economic horizon to take advantage of the straits in which a vast number of Canadian people find themselves, due in no small measure to the taxation policies of this government, taxation policies which are flagrantly designed to favour those who are already privileged at the expense of those who are reduced to borrowing from these vulture small loans companies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if this is our situation at the present time, and no one can deny it is-certainly there would be no field of operation for these small companies if the ordinary Canadian citizen were getting a larger share of this increase in wealth production-then the situation tomorrow may be very much worse. It may very well be that the already inequitable and extremely dangerous economic division of wealth in Canada will be still further distorted by developments that are now taking place in industry. The other day I was interested to note that one of the contributions of the Department of National Health and Welfare to the health and welfare of the Canadian people was the installation of automatic machinery for calculating and making out

The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron cheques. It is a very efficient piece of machinery. It now requires only 286 man or woman hours in place of the 15,000 man or woman hours that were required by previous procedures in making out these cheques. I am not for one moment complaining of the department installing this modern equipment, but I do suggest we should be asking ourselves, what is to become of the people who are displaced? We should be asking ourselves whether the Department of National Health and Welfare is solving its problem by, shall we say, eliminating the necessity for family allowance cheques in the near future by eliminating the possibility of Canadian couples raising families.
This is one of the things that is going to increase this disparity, because the installation of equipment of this type in ordinary business enterprises is undertaken for one purpose only, and that is to cut down on the total disbursements in wages and salaries. There is no other purpose for it. The efficient and competent business manager is, of course, by the very nature of his position, bound to be looking around for means to reduce his payroll. He would not hold his job very long if he were not doing that. Ominously enough, today there is apearing on the scene an array of innumerable types of equipment which will enable the economical, the up and coming business manager, to reduce the total volume of wage disbursements. Then we may find the Minister of Finance introducing a budget and presenting us with a white paper that will no longer be able to say that the increase in labour income accounted for 55 per cent of the total increase in personal income. As a matter of fact I thought that was a scandalous enough admission to make when we consider that the employed class in Canada is by far the largest section of our community. Approximately 4 million people are engaged in working for wages and salaries, yet their increase in personal income only amounted to 55 per cent of the total increase in personal income in this country.
Those are some of the problems that are presented to us, and some future minister of finance is going to have to face them. I believe, sir, even our present minister may be going to face some more difficulties in the future, and I wonder if he perhaps has some uneasy inkling of it. I was very interested in finding that Canada's Minister of Finance, in introducing his budget, made no reference either oblique or direct by one single word to one item of budgetary expense in this country, an expense that constitutes, or did until recently, almost half our total government spending. I looked in vain through the minister's speech for any reference to the $1,775 million we are proceeding to spend on
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo) .1

defence again this year. I was interested, in looking at the estimates, to find that exactly the same figure is put down this year as was put down last year. Hitherto there have been some variations of a few hundred million, but now this figure of $1,775 million is put down in the estimates. I wonder, sir, if defence spending has become a sort of sacred cow at that particular figure, because of course there is nothing so easily defensible as defence expenditures and nothing so dangerous to criticize. But I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that even our present government in Canada has realized that we are moving into some sort of new era in the world, and that possibly the courses we have followed will be proven to be ineffective in protecting us from the sort of dangers our form of society presents.
The other day I was interested in reading an article by a distinguished British journalist. He pointed out that Great Britain, of course, is now facing the fact that it is not possible for her to develop effective defences. Her only hope is to develop a real and effective disarmament program in the world. I suspect that our Minister of Finance plunked down this nice round sum of $1,775 million for defence because that is the handy thing to do. I suspect he is well aware that in all probability before the next 12 months are out Dr. Solandt or some eminent person will put another banana peel underneath the defence program of Canada and reveal again to the astonished population that all these incredible quantities of money and labour that we have been dedicating to defence are, in fact, money and effort down the drain. The government will have to face the problem of either embarking on a larger, more expensive program of military defence, one which I think is beyond the capacities of a country of our size, or will have to abandon much of the present spending.
Now, of course, that cannot be done without some economic repercussions, and it would not do to have economic repercussions in 1956. But, Mr. Speaker, on the other hand, if in 1957 it were possible to make a good slash in the defence budget, and a corresponding election-pleasing tax reduction, then by the time the government was back again and the inevitable results of severely curtailing our defence expenditure became evident they would be safely back in office again to struggle with it for the next four years.
I remember once suggesting to the minister's predecessor that I thought before the year was out he would reduce defence expenditures by at least $200 million, but the hon. gentleman of course pooh-poohed the idea as ridiculous, as giving way in the face of the enemy. Curiously enough, by the time

that year had elapsed we did find that defence expenditures had been reduced by some $175 million. I shall not be surprised-in fact. I shall be surprised, Mr. Speaker-if next year the Minister of Finance does not place in the estimates a much more realistic and much more believable figure than $1,775 million, a repeat of last year and this year. I suspect we shall find a very large reduction, and we shall be told then, of course, that there has been a tremendous change in the international climate; we shall be told that the cold war is warming up.

Now, I do not object to that, Mr. Speaker, and I fully realize the difficulties of the minister's office; but I would suggest this to him. It would have been a little more convincing if, instead of having again just obviously taking the second sheet from last year's estimates to put in this year's estimates he had, for instance, put down a figure of $1,773,000,253.49, or something like that. We then might have believed that some real, serious thought had been given to our defence budget. I myself find it very difficult to believe in the reality of this very apt figure when I see it appearing again and again, and apparently assuming a' fixed place in our budgetary estimates.
I am prepared to agree that perhaps it is necessary, not merely from the defence point of view but from the point of view of defending the country and defending our economy from a serious reverse, because I always remember, Mr. Speaker, the word of warning that was given to the banking and commerce committee by the deputy minister of finance a couple of years ago. He warned us then that any severe cuts in defence spending would be bound to have very serious repercussions on the Canadian economy.
I will conclude with this, Mr. Speaker. Sooner or later these cuts will have to be made, because not for very much longer are we going to be able to justify these expenditures to the Canadian people. After all, they also read, just as members of parliament do. They read the things that Dr. Solandt tells us, which increasingly makes one wonder just what is happening up on the D.E.W. line, whether there is any purpose in going on with it. The Canadian people are reading these things and before very long they are going to ask for something more than the statement that it is going to cost $1,775 million to defend us from the Russians. They are going to want to know, for instance, whether there is any reasonable expectation that this expenditure can protect us from
The Budget-Mr. Bruneau the Russians, and whether there is any reasonable case to be made out for it.
I submit, sir, that the case is becoming shakier and shakier. Then this government will have to face a very difficult situation. They will have to face the curtailment of expenditures that have been a major factor in our economy in the post-war period.
I only hope, sir, that the Minister of Finance has some more detailed plans for dealing with that situation than by continuing to give tax exemption credits to dividends and by continuing to permit the piling up of profits to an extent that is unequalled in our history. I hope the minister is going to take some very definite and serious steps to redistribute income in Canada, not merely from the point of view of equity and justice but from the point of view of economic survival, because I suggest to you, sir, that the present income division and the present shaky foundation of our economic prosperity, based on this magic figure of $1,775 million, is far too dangerous for us to continue indefinitely.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget now under study and the tax policy proposed for the next fiscal year reflect, I am sure, a tendency toward a healthy economy and financial security for our country at large. With a gross national product yielding about $28 billion in 1956 and a tax structure which will bring in revenue of about $4,775 million and possible expenditures of about $4,650 million, we shall have a surplus of about $125 million. One will then readily understand that in these exacting times, with commitments under the NATO scheme and the Colombo plan, with our national defence preparedness and our schemes of social security, one would be justified in summing up the criticism regarding the present fiscal policy with the Shakespearean expression, "Much ado about nothing".
The economic stability toward which all government policies are directed can be considered, I think, as the cornerstone of our national life. The budget before the house leaves us with no doubt as to the good effects of the policies applied in every field by a wise government, and the people of Canada are also entitled to a share of commendation for these achievements.
As the Minister of Finance very justly pointed out in his budget speech, "Careful judgment and wise spending policies are not solely a matter of concern to public authorities. Those are responsibilities of each one of us, regardless of his role in the economy". As a rule we can say that the people of

The Budget-Mr. Bruneau Canada are co-operating fully with those they have selected to conduct the affairs of the country. Among other things, I noticed in the speech of the Minister of Finance the interest of the government in the credit unions and co-operatives, saving and lending societies. Important unions and co-operatives and companies of that kind are operating in my constituency, and I know what they mean to the average farmer as well as to the average citizen. I firmly believe that the intention of the government is to help these organizations to acquire an even more stable financial basis, and they have taken an important step in that direction. The extension to them of privileges and opportunities which were not open to them until now will surely greatly benefit the population at large.
Before speaking on other points arising from the budget speech and from the general financial position of the country, may I note with pleasure the hint given by the Minister of Finance as to the possible salary increases of the federal civil servants. If these increases are granted they will represent large sums of money, and together with other large additional expenses the government will have to face during the next fiscal year I think they will represent a considerable accomplishment in realizing the prospective surplus of $113 million especially if we consider that there will be a $12 million decrease in sales taxes assessed at the manufacturers' level, and also considering the fact that the provinces will receive much higher revenues guaranteed under the federal tax sharing offer.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to touch upon a few subjects which are of particular interest to my constituents. I would feel guilty and my constituents would be justified in blaming me if I did not mention the interest we all have in the ways and means of assuring peace in the world. We are among those who believe that our country has really been working toward peace through the actions of this government. Canada has been and will continue to be one of the main supporters of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. We believe the reason for the government's policy is that Canada cannot live as a contented nation if the peace of another important part of the world is in jeopardy from the forces that seek to bring about the destruction of civilization. In NATO we find the basic ideas of "Liberte, egalite, frater-nite" as they were laid down nearly 175 years ago, but there is something more. There is the survival of democratic ideals as they exist now, no matter how different from the original version they may be. Canada has


taken a definite stand to defend these principles and what has been acquired through them. We feel that NATO is the body that can do so.
The Minister of Finance has emphasized these basic concepts in his budget speech by asking parliament to appropriate important credits for Canada's participation in NATO and for the implementation of a strong national defence program. We must first secure peace for the people of the world and for ourselves as Canadians.
The reasons for which peace must be secured are obvious. There is scarcely any need to explain why Canadians want peace, aside from the fact that they are human beings. Canada knew prosperity in time of war; it remains that our well-being depends mainly on a sound normal economy. Moreover, peace cannot be preserved solely by force of arms. Canada has devoted much effort in helping the underdeveloped countries by participating in the Colombo plan. Many of my constituents have suggested that the government should allocate an extra amount of $9 million toward that end.
I would like to thank and congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs for having asked the house to vote an additional $8 million for the Colombo plan. Perhaps you would allow me, sir, to congratulate the various women's groups of Glengarry-Prescott for bringing to my attention resolutions to that effect.
Now, what about our economy? To obtain as high a degree of prosperity as possible, the government during recent years has adopted a series of measures aimed at achieving a fairer distribution of wealth amongst the various classes of our society and bringing a higher degree of well-being and security to all. In the economic field particularly measures have been implemented to increase production and dispose of our products on the markets of the world, as well as on our own markets.
Unfortunately there are still many sectors of our economy where there is over production, where the producers have to struggle hard in order to make a living and keep their industries alive. This government is fully aware of that fact and has proved it by asking this house to vote guarantees for bank loans to producers secured by their grain, in order to provide an immediate source of funds where they may be needed, and also by authorizing the treasury to bear the cost from August 1, 1955, of storage and interest charges on wheat held by the wheat board over and above its normal carryover levels.
I for one approved with pleasure such measures, but as the representative of a very

important dairy producing area of eastern Canada, I feel that the dairy industry should also receive help and protection by means of subsidies proportionate to the money spent to help the western grain farmers. It is not a case of saying, "They received an apple; we also want one." There is a real need for such help among the dairy producers.
Incidentally, on that matter may I draw to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture correspondence received from various agricultural organizations in my riding requesting that the present 58 cent floor price on butter be maintained. This is one of the measures for which the government is to be commended, and I wish at this time to thank the Minister of Agriculture for maintaining this policy in force.
I wish now to speak about the cattle breeders of eastern Canada. I need not emphasize here the difficulties met by these groups in finding markets for their production at reasonable prices and in meeting the competition from western Canadian producers as well as that from other countries. Like the wheat growers, the cattle breeders constitute an important part of the Canadian economy, and as such their industry should be kept healthy in the interests of the entire Canadian economy. For that matter I might mention that the hog producers of this part of the province are now operating at a not too encouraging profit.
In the agricultural field I am glad to note that' the government has asked parliament to increase the amount of loans which may be made by the Canadian farm loan board, and that it is seeking to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
I have here, sir, a brief which was sent to me by the secretary of the Glengarry federation of agriculture, submitted by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in which it is stated that it is their hope that the government will encourage and assist financially the development of programs to regularly provide milk to children in primary and secondary schools. The brief also points out that it seems hardly reasonable that on one hand Canada should support all sections of the milk industry through its butter support program, and at the same time have in effect a special nominal rate of duty on imports of skim milk powder and cheese from what is perhaps the lowest cost producing area in the world, namely New Zealand. In order to permit Canadian producers to fully develop their home market the federation recommended that the special tariff agreement with Australia and New Zealand be revised to raise the present duty on cheese to an effective level, and to bring the duties on skim milk from those countries to 3J cents per
The Budget-Mr. Bruneau pound. Further, until such time as these duties are imposed, arrangements should be made to use the Export and Import Permits Act to control imports of cheddar cheese and skim milk powder.
The brief asked that the federal butter aid program for institutions be further explored and continued, and that a plan be established for distributing dairy products such as milk and butter to certain categories of needy people by the use of coupons which could only be used for the purchase of those commodities; and that adequate protection be provided against cheap imported edible oils and against products from which edible oils can jae obtained.
This brings me to the industrial problems our country is now facing. First may I say that the government was never so well advised as when it asked for an extension to the scope of the industrial development bank.
(Translation):
As our good friend, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Laflamme) has so rightly mentioned, when seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the government, in widening the field of activity of the industrial development bank will certainly promote the development of lesser industries. I entirely agree with him when he stresses that increased government assistance to lesser industries would be of very great help in solving the problems of unemployment and housing. But I shall go further than that.
(Text):
The growth of small industries is necessary to the survival of older urban districts like the one I represent in this house, but in addition I firmly believe that the decentralization of industry is necessary if we are to solve the acute problems of unemployment and housing and secure stability for the Canadian economy. For instance, we all know that in eastern Canada the bulk of industry is centralized in the main cities, leaving dozens of other areas with a second-class economy and a rather lean population. Because of this situation I contend that a large proportion of the population of Canada situated in villages, towns and small cities is not getting a just share of the high standard of living which this country is now experiencing. In those villages, towns and small cities the income is generally lower and the incidence of unemployment is higher than anywhere else. In some cases these unemployed people probably find temporary or sporadic work in the large centres; but speaking as a human being, who would want to leave his own town and his family in order to go away and live sometimes under deplorable conditions in a strange city? In

The Budget-Mr. Bruneau any event the housing situation that exists in many industrial areas is enough to keep anyone away unless forced by starvation to make such a move.
It is all very well to attempt to encourage home improvement by increasing the amount of the loans available for this purpose, and to encourage the redevelopment of older sections of large cities, but the fact remains that many cities and urban areas are overcrowded and the general feeling is that no solution will be found for these problems until other areas and cities are thought of in considering the decentralization of industry.
For instance, in my own constituency of Glengarry-Prescott there are scores of communities possessing facilities for the establishment of new industries or the re-establishment of previously existing industries. Geographically speaking, we are located exactly halfway between Montreal and Ottawa. The lines of the two great Canadian railways cross the constituency, which is quite active economically. I submit that this would be an ideal spot for the establishment of new industry or the relocating of industries already established. We have unemployed people who would benefit from these new industries, and we also have the space available for the building of homes. The moving of industry to Glengarry-Prescott would certainly help our people, and it would also serve to assist the heavy industrial zones by freeing housing units and preventing newcomers worsening the housing situation in those cities and their suburban areas.
While I am speaking for my own constituency, I know there are dozens of other constituencies which could also offer good industrial facilities and which would like to have a fairer share of Canada's prosperity. I believe it is high time that industry should break the economic barrier of large cities where factories are clustered together, and migrate to the smaller places available in our spacious country.
However, this does not mean that the people do not appreciate the latest amendments to the housing act enacted by the government, which will permit them to borrow larger amounts for the making of payments on new homes. Every day more and more people are taking advantage of the provisions of the housing act, but it is our contention that the decentralization of industry would do much to alleviate this problem of home construction which Canada is now facing in the large as well as in the small communities.
Moreover, is it not recognized that the decentralization of industry is an important

asset to national security? According to studies in business policy as published by the national industrial conference board, many United States enterprises have followed this line. This publication quotes an executive of a big company as follows:
National security considerations have entered into our selection of new plant sites to a certain extent. Given the choice between two otherwise equal locations, we have chosen sites not too close to large centres of population or other possible targets.
The same publication states:
During world war II a decided shift in the sizes of towns chosen for increased industrial activity became evident. Almost half the factories of the large multi-plant companies co-operating in a conference board survey made in 1948 were situated, prior to 1940, in cities of more than 100,000 population. Only one-fifth are in towns of less than 10,000 and less than one-third were located in medium-size cities of 10,000 to 100,000 persons.
During the eight years 1940 through 1947, however, a radical change in the pattern set in. Small and medium-size towns became much more popular throughout the nation, to the detriment of the large urban centres, according to co-operating companies. As a result, by the end of 1947, large, medium-size and small communities each had accounted for an almost equal share of the reported wartime expansions involving construction and purchase of new plants.
Along with this may I point out that decentralization would also be to the advantage of the companies themselves. Finally, on the matter of national security as well as economic stability I should like to quote a representative of a big textile manufacturer, who says:
Decentralization spreads the risk of conflagration and catastrophe. Because we produce a national brand line, continuity of service is paramount in our company.
For the above mentioned reasons I should like to direct the attention of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce to this problem, and make a suggestion to the government. My suggestion is that the government consider immediately the possibility of working out a master plan for the decentralization of industry. The problem is most urgent and wide-ranging. I would suggest the appointment during this session of a committee, independent of the commission on economic prospects, to investigate and study the situation and report to the government.
Among my reasons for speaking of a decentralized industry was the general welfare of the people. From that same motive I would like to point out the importance of establishing as soon as possible a health insurance scheme from coast to coast, in cooperation with the provincial governments. I know I do not have to convince the members of this house that such a plan is essential if we are to live up to the expectancies of our social standards. I wanted to stress our hope

that enough provinces will concur to implement the scheme put forward by the federal government so it can benefit as early as possible those who cannot afford the inevitable luxury of illness on an average salary.
I am happy to state here that I was in-, formed that 8,000 acres of peat bog land near Alfred, 40 miles east of Ottawa, are being reclaimed for a multi-million dollar development to supply eastern Ontario and United States markets with prepackaged and frozen produce. The development is expected to employ between 600 and 800 people, most of them on a year-round basis, and a good many more at the height of seasonal production. Trenching crews have been working this winter setting up drainage routes. Fourteen miles have been completed.
For the past 10 or 15 years the Alfred bog has been looked upon as useless, but now developments in horticulture have made its development look more feasible. There has been a peat development, but the market for the peat is small. There was a small experimental development in market produce at the Caledonia Springs end of the bog, but a peat fire ended this. Large amounts of capital on which there can be no return for three or four years are going into the development.
Before closing I would like to say a few words on a subject which I have always had at heart, that of the possible creation of a national department of youth. Nearly every session since I have been elected to this house I have advocated such a move by the government. I now feel it is more urgent than ever. Canada now has passed the crossroads of its destiny, but we must see to it that tomorrow will not force us to turn back. No matter how sound and healthy our policy is today, we are bound to a collapse if the young men and women of today are not adequately prepared to take over from our present leaders and tackle the problems that lie ahead of us. I am thinking, for instance, of extending to as many as possible a fair opportunity to go ahead in life. Without interfering with the provincial rights in education, through appropriate arrangements between governments a system of scholarships could be established on a national basis to help those who have talent but no money to take their full share of duties and advantages in Canadian life.
In this connection may I point out that the national federation of Canadian university students, which represents over 50,000 students at more than 20 Canadian universities, has been and still is conducting a campaign in that direction in order to help deserving university students. The students are seeking the payment of bursaries and scholarships in
23, 1956	2575
The Budget-Mr. Bruneau the form of 2,500 annual awards, each tenable for four years. Fully under way, such a program is estimated to cost approximately $5,500,000. The federation feels such an objective is broad enough to assist "valuable good students as well as the merely brilliant, but not so broad as to be revolutionary". Personally I think $5,500,000 is not an exaggerated sum to be devoted to the preparation of our leaders of tomorrow. Other countries are devoting much more money than that to the same purpose; and some of them, we must agree, do not have the same need for it as we have, being older and bigger countries than Canada.
This is only one point. As you know, there are many others that can be integrated in a homogeneous program to be administered by a new department of youth. Such a department, I understand, cannot be created from thin air, and would require a certain shifting in the present governmental departments and services. A thorough study should be given to the matter by government experts in cooperation with lay organizations specializing in the problems of youth, in order to define exactly which part of the administration should be entrusted to the new minister of youth. In order to prevent too great a disturbance in the present administrative services, I would suggest that to start with the new department could be entrusted to a minister already appointed. The hon. Secretary of State, for instance, would be a logical choice.
The government realizes fully, I know, the utmost importance of bringing our youth to the level of the heavy responsibilities they are to face in the future, and I am sure they will neglect nothing to reach that goal. The good administration of a country undoubtedly is to be found in healthy internal and external policies in the economic and diplomatic fields, but this cannot attain long-range success without adequate protection and development of the fundamental human values that are to be found in the younger generations.
Peace at any cost to preserve mankind and our Canadian way of life; a sound policy to spur our growing economy and secure a still happier life for our people, and the preparation for the future by adequate help to our youth-these are a few of the general ideas that in my estimation should be considered as paramount at the present time, and I hope the suggestions I have respectfully submitted to the government will be of some use.
While a budget may not always be to the liking of the cross-section of the people of Canada represented here in this House of Commons, one must not forget that a stable

If one will glance at Hansard of less than half a century ago, the budget tabled in this very house had to do with expenditures of about $6 million, covering but a few federal departments and an administration that presented but very few intricate problems.
Today-and I am sure, sir, all the members in this house, including those of the various opposition parties, will agree the social and economic life of the country is very closely interwoven with the pattern of federal government, and my colleagues here will vouch to that by the innumerable problems brought to their attention in their relations with their constituents. While we would like to see more measures implemented and more schemes enacted, I believe the people we represent in this house will forgo some improvement for the time being in order to assure security and a more stable economy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to discuss today just one item among the proposals made by the Minister of Finance in his budget address. It is an item, however, of rather far reaching implications in what was an otherwise not too noteworthy speech on government policy.
I refer to the minister's proposal to impose a special 20 per cent excise tax on all revenues from advertising received by Canadian editions of foreign-owned publications. These include the Canadian edition of Time magazine, Reader's Digest, and several trade and women's shopping magazines. This proposal is, in my opinion, a proposal for an iniquitous and dishonest tax, discriminatory in its application and wrong and dangerous in principle.
I hold no brief for the American-owned publications affected. Of some I am a regular reader. Others 1 seldom if ever see. By the same token I am a regular purchaser and reader of a number of Canadian periodicals for whose particular benefit this proposed tax on certain of their competitors has been concocted. Some of them, like Maclean's, Saturday Night and New Liberty, occupy a notable place in the Canadian publication world, and are a part of Canadiana I would like to see continue; but not at the expense of imposing a tax on their competitors as unfair and unsound as that contemplated. Later in my remarks I will suggest some constructive alternatives to this tax proposal.
It is perhaps especially appropriate that I speak my mind on this issue, for in addition to being a Canadian with a strong desire to see our country grow soundly and well,
I am also a publisher and editor of certain Canadian-owned trade journals each of which


competes, and reasonably successfully too, against both Canadian and foreign publications, with many of these competitors enjoying greater advantages by way of financial strength, advertising revenues, circulation and printing facilities than do the publications in which I have a personal interest.
If the principles involved in the proposed excise tax were to be generally accepted by Canada, by their application to more than just the Canadian editions of certain United States-owned journals, there would be a sharp reduction in the advantages now enjoyed by competitors of the publications in which I have an interest, and thus potentially there would be financial gain and lessened competition for my publications.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: I am not suggesting that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would prefer to meet competition by continuing to try to persuade readers and advertisers of the merits of the publications themselves, rather than have my competitors handicapped by unfair restrictions imposed on them by government. The government's sole justification for its proposed tax is that this extraordinary step is necessary in order that Canadian magazines may successfully compete with Canadian editions of foreign-owned magazines. Actually it cannot be logically assumed that financial success and thus the continuance of Canadian magazines would automatically result by imposing a special and heavy tax burden on the competing United States-owned Canadian editions.
Some of these so-called "maple leaf" editions that would be hit by the 20 per cent tax levy might decide to call it quits, in which case scores of thousands of Canadians who now buy these magazines because of the added Canadian material content as well as the basic United States material would be the losers, and also the Canadian tax collector would be the loser. But it does not necessarily follow that the partial vacuum in places to spend advertising budgets would or could be filled by the Canadian magazines who have demanded this legislation. Advertisers put their money into media where they believe the best results can be obtained. They have a wide choice between Canadian and United States periodicals, newspapers, radio, television, direct mail, signboards and so on.
On the other hand, perhaps the publishers of some of these "maple leaf" editions might incorporate all or a large part of the proposed excise tax in their advertising rates, and thus force each Canadian advertiser to make his own decision. He would have to decide whether to carry on in the same publications by increasing his advertising budget or by cutting down his expenditures

in other media; or, in the reverse, by cutting out his advertisements in "maple leaf" editions and using his budget in other media. It is quite possible that Canadian magazines might lose advertising and thus worsen their revenue position if advertisers stick by higher cost "maple leaf" edition space.
On the other hand, there is no assurance whatsoever that a cut-back in "maple leaf" advertising would go to Canadian magazines rather than into newspaper, radio, television or other advertising media. Each medium has to sell its own case to advertisers on its own merits, and there is certainly no assurance that those who seek this restrictive excise tax can garner for themselves extra advertising revenue from its application to a limited few of their competitors.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, a third possibility if this excise tax is applied would be incorporation into reader costs, that is into the single copy sale price or subscription rates, of the tax or a large part of the tax. Under these circumstances scores of thousands of Canadians would be asked to pay the price of giving certain Canadian publishers the protection they want, or else readers could give up buying "maple leaf" editions for which they have developed a taste. Whatever decision readers may make would not guarantee even a single copy increase in the circulation of the Canadian magazines which seek this tax on their competitors.
The announced purpose of the special tax is to help keep purely Canadian magazines in business by imposing a special burden on certain of their relatively successful competitors, the Canadian editions of United States magazines. I submit there is no assurance that the tax can or will achieve its stated objective, nor has the Minister of Finance submitted any evidence that the publications for which he seeks help actually need it.
Are Maclean's, Saturday Night, New Liberty and other Canadian magazines making money or losing money? Have they done and are they now doing a good enough job in setting up their product in a format and with material sufficiently appealing to Canadian readers? Are they doing a good enough job in selling the merits of their publications to Canadian advertisers? If they are falling down on their job, there is even less excuse for imposing a discriminatory tax upon certain of their competitors.
If the proposed tax fails to give these Canadian magazines the kind of profits they would
The Budget-Mr. Nickle like to enjoy, then what would they seek next by way of cutting down competition for the advertisers' dollar? Well, Canadian daily newspapers, weekly newspapers, such weekly supplements as Weekend Magazine and the Star Weekly, Canadian radio and television stations, have sold advertisers on the merits of using their facilities. If Canadian editions of United States magazines are beaten down to size by the imposition of an excise tax on their advertizing revenue, why not push for the imposition of a similar kind of levy on one or more of the Canadian magazines' other competitors right within Canada? Or maybe we can dream up some kind of legislation to force Canadian advertisers to allocate their advertising budgets among specific media on a basis which will guarantee that Canadian magazines will get a big enough share.
Principal targets of the current special tax are the publishers of the Canadian edition of Time magazine and the publishers of the English and French language editions of Reader's Digest. Both of these are Canadian corporations, although owned by United States parent companies. Both have headquarters in Quebec province. Both pay full Canadian corporate income taxes on 100 per cent of their profits from circulation and advertising in Canada, together with Quebec local taxes. Their liability to tax collectors in Canada is exactly the same as that of the Canadian-owned publications.
Reader's Digest prints its two Canadian monthly editions in Montreal, providing a very sizeable addition to the earnings of its Canadian printer and his employees. Time prints its Canadian edition in Chicago, apparently because no Canadian printing company is at present in a position to meet the tight and fast Time schedule essential to a weekly news magazine.
These, then, are the principal targets of today. They are both United States-owned Canadian corporations which share the fruits of their successful enterprise with Canadian tax collectors on exactly the same basis as any other purely Canadian corporation. In addition, when and if they have dividends to pay to their United States parent, they leave an additional withholding tax levy with the dominion tax collector. Well over half their profits thus already wind up in the hands of government in Canada.
Now, in response to demands from Canadian magazines, the government would impose a stiff 20 per cent tax levy on their gross advertising revenue on top of levies already imposed, thus jeopardizing their successful continuance in Canada and perhaps even driving them out of Canada. Drive them out of Canada and they would presumably reach

The Budget-Mr. Nickle north to Canadian readers with regular American editions, on the same basis as the mass of United States publications which are not affected by the proposed excise tax. They would cease to be important contributors to Canadian tax collectors.
