speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the excuse of trying to maintain profits for Canadian magazines, the government proposes a special tax of an entirely new kind on a limited few of the competitors for advertising revenue. This tax is discriminatory because it applies to just a few, not to all. It is a special kind of tax because it marks the first attempt to levy an excise tax on gross revenue from advertising. It is a dangerous tax because it could open the door to discriminatory levies upon other members of the publishing or other industries where competition is intense. It is dangerous also because the precedent established might well lead to the view that special federal taxes on advertising in all its forms is a legitimate source of revenue. It is dishonest because it provides no assurance that its purported objective can be achieved.
The proposal appears to accept the principle that the larger, more successful of competitors should be penalized by special taxes to prevent them becoming too successful against smaller, higher cost and perhaps less efficient companies in the same field. It is a principle that I find little to my liking if we are to have a free competitive society.
Recently Hamilton, Ontario, became a one-newspaper city when one daily newspaper folded up because it could not compete in circulation and advertising revenue with the Hamilton Spectator. If the principle in the new excise tax be right, would it not have been fair to impose a special tax upon the Hamilton Spectator to help its competitor? Might it also then be right to impose a special
[Mr. Nickle.1
tax on advertising revenue on the more successful newspapers in our own Canadian cities, where smaller competitors have rough going? Going further, we might tack on a special levy on the advertising budget of the more successful merchants in order to raise their costs in relation to their smaller competitors. We could, perhaps, have a lot of fun helping to create more chaos in Canada.
In my own field, as a publisher of trade journals in western Canada, we might then give serious consideration to trying to guarantee continuance of this small, healthy prairie province industry by levying a special tax on advertising revenue on the eastern Canadian publishers of somewhat greater financial strength, who compete with us with the aid of lower unit costs and bigger facilities. This Mr. Speaker, would be a levy against at least one of the Canadian publishers who want a special tax put upon certain of their United States competitors.
I do not seriously propose that last suggestion, of course. If I could not successfully compete by fair means, I would sooner go out of business than resort to demands that my competitors have their wings clipped by extraordinary taxes. However, my business like thousands of others in Canada is managing to successfully compete with larger and more powerful ones. I earnestly urge the Minister of Finance to scrap this discriminatory special tax, and advise the Canadian magazine publishers who sought it to find better and fairer means to compete with the "maple leaf" editions.
As the minister pointed out in his budget speech, it is important to Canada that Canadian publications, by Canadians, for Canadians, telling about Canadians, continue to thrive. Like him, sir, I would not happily contemplate a time when we would not have a Canadian magazine; when there would not be an opportunity for persons with the talent and the time to write and contribute articles on government, scientific matters or some other subjects. Like him, sir, I would not happily contemplate a time when our children could not read a magazine in which there would be Canadian stories based on Canadian history, or Canadian fiction. Certainly we all want purely Canadian magazines to continue playing a part in our Canadian culture. I believe they can, and without discriminatory taxes upon their competitors. I would earnestly suggest to the publishers of our Canadian magazines that they get out and do a better job of determining what Canadians find appealing in the periodicals they buy. They should revamp, where it seems necessary, the format, art work and editorial content to attract more Canadian

readers. They should get out and sell Cana-dianism to Canadians through more Canadian content in their magazines. If they sell Cana-dianism effectively, they will sell more magazines.
As to advertising revenue, the flow to Canadian publishers will grow as they sell the merits of their publications to readers. It can also, I am confident, be considerably expanded by a more intense job of selling advertising on the merits of building stronger, better, bigger all-Canadian magazines, and the competitive merits of ads in such publications as compared to all the other media available. If Canadian publishers cannot effectively sell the merits of their periodicals to Canadians readers and advertisers, then they do not deserve permanent existence.
It seems to me there is one way at least in which co-operation between Canadian government and publishers could now help build a sounder national magazine industry and encourage the development of more Canadian creative writing talent. What I have in mind might be called a Canadian creative writing fund, to which government and publishers would contribute each year an equal amount, perhaps $50,000 to $100,000 each. This joint government-industry fund would, under a board of qualified editors and authorities on Canadiana, disburse annual grants in monthly contests for fact and fiction articles, short stories and short novels, Canadian in theme and written by Canadians. I would envisage monthly awards for first, second and third best in each category of writing, being at least comparable to the fees now paid authors by the leading Canadian magazines. Such awards would be treated as payment for the title to the winning articles and stories. The Canadian creative writing fund award winning stories could then be allocated on an equitable basis to Canadian magazines, on the basis of their contribution to the fund, and each story would then become the property of and be published by that magazine.
This proposed measure of government subsidy in a joint effort with Canadian publishers to encourage Canadian writing talent would, I believe, be money well spent in the national interest. It would create a pool of Canadian stories and articles to supplement the editorial material acquired in the normal way by Canadian magazines and could, I believe, contribute substantially to awakening broader interest among the Canadian public and Canadian advertisers in supporting Canadian magazines featuring Canadian material designed for Canadian tastes.
In conclusion, and to get back to the special tax proposed in the budget, may I remind the government of the rightful indignation felt
Private Bills
by Canadians a short time ago when the legislature of the state of Maryland passed a measure discriminating specifically against a Canadian company desiring to build a plant and compete with United States firms in that area. Like most Canadians, the United States state department found the discrimination distasteful and unwise, as did the governor of Maryland. This week the governor of Maryland vetoed the bill. I suggest that this government's proposed discriminatory excise tax on Canadian editions of United States magazines will rouse as much rightful indignation in the United States as the Maryland bill did here in Canada. Let us therefore take a leaf from the Maryland governor's book and kill an unfair measure before it ever becomes law in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day the leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, referred to a report of Mr. MacGregor, the head of the department of insurance, dealing with the increased interest shown by United States loan companies in the very lucrative Canadian field. He pointed out at that time that there had been increasing United States interest in this field through the provincially incorporated subsidiary companies of United States loan concerns. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is a matter which deserves the very close attention of hon. members.
There have been a number of other events during the past year which have tended to point out the importance of a very close appraisal of Canada's economic position, particularly with respect to the growing United States control of Canadian business. Issues are before this house at the present time. There is the question of the gas pipe line. There are other instances which ought to be a clear warning to all Canadians' that we owe it to ourselves to give the closest attention to any proposal which might, even in the slightest degree, increase the extent of outside control over Canadian business.
The people of the United States are much more concerned about protecting their own

Private Bills
interests than we Canadians are in protecting our interests. We in this country have no watchdog such as the federal power commission to protect the consumers of natural gas in this country. In a previous debate an hon. member spoke of a recent event in the state of Maryland where, failing some regulatory body to protect a particular industry in that state, the state legislature had taken action to prevent a Canadian company from engaging in normal business there. In these circumstances I think we cannot allow a bill of this kind to go through this house without giving it our most careful consideration.
As the result of past indecision and lack of concern on the part of this government we have now arrived at the stage where some 83 per cent of the loan business of this country is controlled by two large United States corporations. These two large United States loan companies made profits last year of some $4,800,000. This is money, savings you might call it, which has been drained off to the United States, savings which might under normal circumstances have been available for investment in this country. Indeed, we have had ample indication in recent times of an apparent shortage of investment capital in this country.
These two large companies, having made just under $5 million of Canadian money out of Canadian citizens who had the misfortune to have to go to them and pay the exorbitant interest rates charged, have contributed what to the economy of this country? Have they assisted in the development of our natural resources? The answer is obviously no. Have they in any way contributed to the building up of the industrial capacity of this country? The answer again is no.

subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext: How do you know?

subtopic: SIGNATURE LOAN AND FINANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
What have these companies done? They have come into this country; they have borrowed Canadian money from Canadian banks at lower rates of interest; they have lent this Canadian money to Canadian citizens at exorbitant rates of interest, and as a result of that operation they made profits last year of just under $5 million.
This company may argue that it is performing some service to the people of this country. Certainly it cannot argue that it is contributing to the economic well-being of Canada by preying on misfortune. They are not performing a service in any way. The loans they make are not contributing to the building up of Canada's industrial capacity. The argument is sometimes raised-it was raised in connection with another bill asking for a change in the name of a company-that they are performing some sort of service to the

man on the street. Well, in previous debates we have had the question of the profits of small loans companies discussed. It appears quite obvious that these companies are not in business out of a desire to help the people of Canada.
The small loans field is extremely lucrative. Mark this. Statements were made on previous occasions when private bills were brought in by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that if you go too far and reduce the interest rate too much you are going to drive these people out of business. Well, what is the situation? When the government at long last took some steps toward scaling down the burden on prospective borrowers, this company became anxious to get into the field, which certainly proves that at the present time the field is lucrative enough to attract outside firms to enter it.
In a previous debate some reference was made to the nature of the advertising carried on by those firms. I believe the hon. member for Assiniboia read into the record a number of advertisements. Of course, the most memorable was the one entitled, "You are my pal". The two companies I have referred to control 83 per cent of the small loans field in Canada, and they spent over $1 million on just that type of advertising. Hon. members will agree it is regrettable that any Canadian has to borrow money from a loan company, and that it is a matter of great misfortune. But when a firm, in order to make profits, will go out into the field and do whatever it can to sell the idea of going into debt, that makes the situation well nigh intolerable.
The position in which we find ourselves at the moment is simply this. No one can argue that there are not enough loan companies in the field in Canada today. No one can argue that this field is controlled by Canadian companies. It is not simply a question of having another firm coming in to do business. It is simply a question of adding to the heavy preponderance of this business which is being conducted by firms with headquarters outside of this country.
Of course when they come before parliament seeking incorporation they have very able and very influential people acting on their behalf. I have noted the names mentioned in this bill. One name which is mentioned is that of Duncan Kenneth MacTavish, the president of the national Liberal federation.

I suggest there is a more important principle than the mere passage of this bill. I suggest that at this time we should review our whole attitude toward this problem, which has been brought to the fore during this session to a greater degree perhaps than in previous sessions. Canadian industry today is becoming increasingly dominated by outside capital.
I suggest that my hon. friends on the other side of the house should read a speech made in the other place by a former member of this house, who had some extremely caustic remarks to make concerning this particular bill when it was before the other place. The situation was put quite clearly at that time by the hon. gentleman. He made

One so-called Canadian company sold, in one year, more than $210 million worth of goods to the Canadian public. Over 99 per cent of the stock of that company is owned by the parent company in the United States. The profits from this fairly substantial operation are simply lumped in with the profits of the total sales of the parent company. And Canadians, in order to participate in this company, are forced to purchase stock of the parent company in which they may have no specific interest. Another large and respected subsidiary operating in Canada for many years and completely owned and controlled by the parent U.S. company does not even release Canadian sale figures.
I commend this address to all hon. members of this house. Dr. Hall made this further comment:
Two-thirds of all motor vehicles sold to Canadians last year were produced by companies operating in Canada without Canadian stock. The profits, again, are lumped in with the profits of their giant U.S. parent companies. The dividends paid by the parent company do not reflect Canadian sales nor the position of that company in the Canadian economy.
In summing up later on, Dr. Hall said:
Canada produces 90 per cent of the world's supply of a certain mineral, yet where is the effective head office of that industry's largest company, whose mines are manned by Canadians, whose furnaces are operated by Canadians, and whose profits are made in Canada? Not in Canada, but in one of the cities of the United States. And the Canadian stockholders are paid, not in Canadian dollars, but in U.S. funds!
I maintain that insistence upon the fact that we Canadians should pay attention to this tendency is not expressed exclusively in this particular quarter of the house. I suggest that the former hon. member of this house to whom I referred a moment ago has made what is perhaps one of the best speeches that has been made on the subject, in which he pointed out the danger inherent in this practice. I hope that his colleagues in this house will read his speech and take it to heart. I also quoted from Dr. Hall's remarks. One could go on and quote a great many eminent Canadians who have brought to the attention of the public precisely the same problem.
I suggest that we should give extremely serious consideration to this tendency at this time. If we do not, what is going to happen? It is only a matter of time until not merely 85 per cent but 95 or 100 per cent of the small loans field will be controlled by outside companies. In other forms of economic development in this country we are going to have increasing United States control. The time is coming when the entire economy of Canada

This is a problem which has to be met on a wide front, and I have mentioned merely one aspect of the problem. I do suggest, however, that we have here a specific instance in which we can do something to register our concern and our protest against this alarming tendency. Mr. Speaker, the bill which is presently before the house is relatively uncomplicated. May I say to the house before proceeding any further that if the hon. member who just spoke felt that I did not wish to stand up and explain the bill, he was wrong. The Speaker quite properly caught his eye before he caught mine. Because the hon. member has been in this house for a somewhat longer time than I have, I was prepared to yield to the normal demands of common courtesy.
As to the general argument which the hon. member has made about non-Canadian capital, I submit that there is a place where that might well be discussed. As a member of this house I would be prepared to discuss it at that time, but I suggest with all respect that that is not the point to be raised in respect to this particular bill.
May I say just a word or two in explanation of this bill. Hon. members of this house know full well that in the modern economy of Canada, business may be carried on by a sole proprietorship, by a partnership or, as is the case in a great many instances, by a corporation. Second, most of us here know full well that the great majority of federal corporations are incorporated under the Companies Act, a statute of this parliament, and we know also that certain types of business such as insurance, railway and loan companies must obtain special charters from this parliament, the latter under the Small Loans Act of 1939.
Most hon. members know that the Small Loans Act has been on the statute books of this country since 1939. We know also that there is before us Bill No. 51 to be considered at this session, under which the rates and certain clauses of that act will be up for review. Part II of that act invites any group of people of competence, of character and of experience to present a petition and

application to this house for incorporation as a small loans company. I submit that such a group has a right to be heard by this house.
The form of the bill is very simple, and is prescribed by part II of the Small Loans Act, 1939. Under that act a great many clauses of the Loan Companies Act are made applicable to the Small Loans Act. The majority of the directors of any such company must be Canadian citizens and residents. The overriding Loan Companies Act states that the administration of all these companies, including small loan companies, must be only by the board of directors, the majority of whom, as I have said, must be Canadian citizens and residents.
The bill provides for the incorporation of this company with head office in Ottawa. The company is to have a relatively modest capital in this field of $500,000, which may be increased to $1,000,000. There are to be five directors, the majority of whom will be Canadian citizens and residents. Reference was recently made in this house to the name of a small loan company. In the event that hon. members are anxious to know why this particular company has chosen this particular name, may I say that the sponsor of the bill is the Merchants' Acceptance Corporation, which has carried on business in the New England states since 1909. My understanding is that the sponsors of the bill would have preferred to use the name of the parent company, but the report of the superintendent of insurance states that there is already a company in Canada which uses the word "Merchants". Therefore the sponsors of this bill had to consider some other name and they chose a name which I submit is quite proper, Signature Loan and Finance Company.
This indicates that the person, unfortunately if you will, who needs to borrow $100, $150, $200 or $300, can go to this company for such loan on the basis of his personal character and financial integrity as represented by his signature, and as in the case of all of us that would be his warrant for such a loan. That is the explanation of this bill. As I said, the sponsoring company has carried on business since 1909, mainly in the New England states, and if it is incorporated it proposes to carry on business in Canada principally in eastern Canada.
I said I was not going to be drawn into the general discussion to which the hon. member who spoke last referred. Let me remind all hon. members that while the superintendent of insurance made reference to the growing interest of non-Canadians and Canadians in this field, there are only four small loan companies in Canada under

federal supervision. If the hon. member is sincere, as I expect he is, and if he would prefer that 83 per cent of the small loans business in Canada be not controlled by two of those four companies, I submit that here is an opportunity for another relatively small group to come into Canada. If they feel they can do business here, let them have that opportunity.
I speak only as a member of parliament who is sponsoring this bill on behalf of some of my friends. This is not by any manner or means a Liberal measure, a Conservative measure, a Social Credit measure or a C.C.F. measure. Having been asked by people whom I regard as competent and intelligent to stand up in parliament and sponsor a bill which is being presented because the Small Loans Act of 1939 invites people to come here and carry on business under our Canadian economy, I make this explanation. People in all parts of the world are being urged to enter our favourable economic climate, and it is no wonder that they want to come to Canada. They feel that they want to do business here.
As we know, the undertaker will come for all of us, but I am not for punishing undertakers. There are certain people in Canada who feel they must go to a small loan company for certain reasons, and I submit with great respect that this bill warrants second reading and consideration by the banking and commerce committee.

We had some success with that.	I have always
been interested in this from the point of view of the public. Unfortunately it is the people who are less protected educationally, shall we say, through a lack of knowledge of public affairs, who become the victims of this particular type of company.
Again today I would like to say a word about advertising. Sir, you would be greatly surprised to learn that a great deal of the advertising of these people in the local offices in Ottawa has suddenly disappeared. I would not like to say it was something like the government files that we cannot get at, but you cannot get at them today for some reason. A few days ago you could send your stenographer or a House of Commons messenger to the companies and they were delighted to send you literature. I suggest that the particular type of advertising, with the picture of a little child at the foot of the Christmas tree and mother and father going off to Florida on money they get at 24 per cent per annum from these loan companies, is not too dangerous. Surely nobody in this world would be so simple or so naive as to believe that what this particular type of advertising conveys is anything like the truth. But there is a danger in the other type of advertising, and that is why this was first brought up in the house.
As a matter of fact I can tell the house in confidence that one of the first bills I proposed to place on the order paper of this house, a bill about which I consulted my hon. friends in the caucus, would have the effect of compelling any small loans company, or any outfit that insisted upon advertising its willingness to lend money, include in its advertising the amount of interest per annum or the cost per annum on a percentage basis. If that amount were clearly stated in the advertising, I do not think so many people would fall into the trap set for them by the small loans companies of this sort.
They do not know that. The people that are getting these small loans do not realize what they are up against until they are firmly inside the trap and are seekipg a way to get out. Through the urgency of the need for the money, the poverty, the misery and the fear of losing one's job, a man will pay 100 per cent if necessary, under certain conditions, and the people who give them these accommodations are well aware of that fact.
It has always been my plea that this advertising is deceptive, the advertising in which the rate of interest per annum is not stated. You are not told that, but you are told what you have to pay back each month. The average person-and I say this with some knowledge-who has come to me with his troubles did not realize what that rate of interest was when he borrowed that money. It is worded in such a way that it looks like 8 per cent or 11 per cent as the case may be; but the catch is, of course, that the borrower does not have the full use of the money, as advertised, for the complete 12 months. He has the full use of it only for one month, and the amount he has the use of steadily decreases as the months go on, while the monthly payment of interest is the same.
That is my plea. I think it is a good one. I think what these people say is deceptive. The particular pamphlet I have-as I say I do not know whether or not it is obtainable

today-is one that reached my desk some time ago but came to my attention today. It commences by saying:
Reputable lenders-
I presume these people are reputable; some of their competitors are not.
-have hundreds of unsolicited testimonials that tell the real story of the value of the lender to his community. Sometimes the stories are poignant . . .
"Poignant" is a good word. Not only are they poignant but they are tragic, some of the stories I have heard. I had a sheriff come to see me about the state into which these small people get who use these small loans. He sits down with them and tries to arrange a payment per month which seems to be reasonable, by which they can finally meet their obligations. I notice that this one piece of advertising attacks the credit unions. Any man who attacks credit unions, so far as I am concerned, has a battle on his hands, because I am a believer in the functions of the credit union. Anyone who lives in a province where the credit union and co-operative is used to the extent it is used in my province must agree it is a thing that is beneficial to the body politic. They attack the credit union because the credit union, they say, does not pay cash back into the treasury in the form of taxes, and it can only serve the people in the group.
However, it is easy to get into a credit union. All you have to do is borrow some money and you are in. In some of the cooperatives you only have to make a purchase and you are in. So, after all, I do not think their argument is valid. They do not point out that the credit union is a method of borrowing money at cost, in other words that when you go into a credit union, if you pay as high as 1 per cent per month, the profits made by the organization are not shipped out of the country to some corporation in the United States or some other country but are divided among the actual people who borrowed the money. By that method the interest rate they pay is reduced. To me that sounds logical and sensible.
As I have said, this kind of advertising is deceitful, although it is perhaps less deceitful than some of the things I have seen. I notice on the outside this pamphlet has the words, "From an All-Canadian Viewpoint." I expect these people are getting rather touchy about the talk that 83 per cent, or whatever it is, of the small loans field in Canada is controlled by two foreign corporations. I suppose this is that great old free enterprise and competition working about which we hear so much. So they are protesting just like my hon. friend over there has protested.

It seems to me they do perhaps protest too much. They do not state where the money comes from. They do not state, like my hon. friend, who the directors are; but this is the picture, according to them, from an allCanadian viewpoint. That makes us feel a lot better. They have an interesting explanation here of the rates they charge. Here is what they have to say and I want the house to notice this because, after all, my text in the beginning was deceitful advertising, advertising which misrepresents the facts. You know, if these people would come clean and state their case honestly and decently they would be out of business.

speechtext:
What industries have been organized and are operating in Nova Scotia since 1951, through the assistance of the small industries division of defence production?
Answer by: Mr. Howe (Port Arthur):
The small industries division of the Department of Defence Production was created in 1951 to ensure that all segments of Canadian industry, particularly small industry, were given an opportunity to participate in the defence production program. Its chief function was that of a service division, to assist and advise those firms seeking either direct contracts from the Department of Defence Production or subcontracts from the department's prime contractors.
